title: Civil No. 1113 of 2008 (High Court, Trinidad and Tobago)
text:
Page 1 of 33

REPUBLIC OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE
CLAIM NO: CV2008-01113
BETWEEN
GRACE KENNEDY (TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO) LIMITED
CLAIMANT
AND
DHANESHWAR DEOLALL also known as
BHOLA MARAJ
1ST DEFENDANT
AND
PROJECT MANAGEMENT CONSULTANCY SERVICES LIMITED
2ND DEFENDANT

Before the Honourable Madame Justice C. Pemberton
Appearances:
For the Claimant: Mr. C. Kangaloo instructed by Ms. N. Bisram
For the Second Defendant: Mr. K. Garcia instructed by Mr. A. Ramoutar

JUDGMENT

[1]
The Claimant (“GKL”) brought this action to recover certain sums of money
$1,356,830.00 from the Second Defendant (“PMCSL”) together with interest at the rate
of 5.5% per annum from 19th September 2005 until judgment.

Page 2 of 33

[2]
BACKGROUND

GKL is a limited liability company in the provision of financial services, of which foreign
exchange trading is an authorised activity. The First Defendant is Dhaneshwar Deolall,
also known as, Bhola Maraj. I shall refer to him as (BM) is a fraudster, now well known
to all concerned.
[3]
On 14th September 2005 employees of GKL were lured into preparing and parting with a
certified cheque in favour of “Bhola Maraj” drawn on Republic Bank Ltd who were their
bankers. The cheque was in the amount of $3,142,500.00 TT. BM came to GKL’s offices,
presented them with a RBTT Manager’s Cheque in the sum of $500,000.00US. GKL
parted with the Republic Bank TTD Cheque in exchange for the RBTT USD Cheque. BM
therefore made off with TTD cheque. He attempted to withdraw $700,000.00 from
Republic Bank. For reasons unknown, BM returned to GKL seeking to have the RBTT
cheque returned to him. This adventure was fruitless. BM took leave of GKL never to
return.
[4]
The following day 15th September 2005 BM returned to Republic Bank and requested
that the following transactions be made on his behalf:
• Issuance of several Manager’s cheques to
o Himself in the sum of $785,625.00
o Himself in the sum of $571,295.00
o Ryan Singh in the sum of $785,625.00
• Cash in the sum of $1millon.
This request was fruitful.
[5]
On 16th September 2005 BM again made his way to Republic Bank. This time he re-
negotiated the two cheques drawn on himself for a single cheque payable to PMCSL in
the sum of $1,356.830.00.
[6]
PMSCL was a Limited Liability Company providing Project Management and other
services. Its directing mind and management was in the person of Dr Allan Bachan

Page 3 of 33

(“AB”). PMSCL deposited this cheque with its bankers on or around 19th September
2005.
[7]
There is no dispute that these funds are the result of a fraud perpetrated by BM on GKL.
In fact, the saga of these readily admitted fraudulent funds did not end there. PMCSL
treated with this deposit by issuing the following cheques on the said 19th September
2005:
• To Laurie Diaz Construction Company $906,830.00
• To Junior Thomas $60,000.00
[8]
It is not disputed that Laurie Diaz, Junior Thomas and AB are known to each other. The
evidence will show how well.
[9]
In any event, sometime on or around 26th September 2005 GKL was informed that the
RBTT USD cheque was a forgery. It was worthless as a negotiable instrument and had
no cash value.
[10]
Those facts therefore prompted GKL to sue both BM and PMCSL for the return of their
monies represented by the Republic Bank Cheque dated 14th September 2005. Both
parties were served. BM never entered an appearance or a defence. A Default
Judgment was secured. The matter continued against PMCSL for the reliefs stated
above. I recommended that the parties mediate this matter, but was informed at the
Mediation referral Hearing that GKL was disenchanted with my making any such Order.
The matter proceeded to trial.
[11]
PLEADINGS

CLAIMANT’S CLAIM – GKL
These facts were repeated in the Statement of Claim filed on 22nd May
2009. GKL’s claim is couched in the following terms:
(1)
as money had and received by PMCSL to GK’s use and/or
repayment of the said sum by way of restitution;

Page 4 of 33

(2)
an Order for the repayment of the said sum;
(3)
injunctive relief as against PMCSL from “parting with the
said sum… or any part thereof to the Claimant”…
(4)
damages for conversion.
None of the claims was expressed to be in the alternative in the prayer.
[12]
DEFENDANT’S DEFENCE – PMCSL

PMCSL admitted receiving a cheque in the sum of $1,356,830.00. PMCSL stated that
these sums were received as agent. Part of the sums were admittedly paid to Laurie
Diaz Construction Company (“LDCCL”) as principal, the sum of $906,830.00 and the
other part $60,000.00 was paid to Junior Thomas upon instruction of the principal –
LDCCL. These sums were paid out prior to receiving notice of GKL’s claim. All in all
PMCSL is stating that it changed its position in good faith.
[13]
PMCSL is therefore defending its position on the ground that it would be inequitable for
GKL to seek re-payment of those sums from its coffers. In fact GKL is not entitled to
recover the sums as alleged “or at all”. GKL has suffered no loss or damage which
PMCSL must be ordered to make good.
[14]
The defence however does not stop there. It goes on to explain the relationship
between PMCSL and LDCCL, who it describes as “its client” who it “afforded limited
office accommodation” at its offices. Junior Thomas is described as one who “did odd
jobs and errands” for PMCSL “and no more”.
[15]
Mr. Kangaloo gave comprehensive closing submissions. Counsel made reference to the
fact that in its defence, PMCSL stated that it does not continue to retain monies
obtained by the transaction. The evidence disclosed that the sum of $389,563.69
remains in the said account.

Page 5 of 33

[16]
MATTERS AT TRIAL
Before the trial, both Mr. Kangaloo and Mr. Garcia agreed that the sums of money,
unused by PMCSL from the initial deposit and which stood in its bank account belonged
to GKL. GKL is therefore entitled to a judgment of $389,563.69. The two outstanding
issues are those of interest and costs on this amount.
[17]
Further there is no contest that there is an identified trail of movement of
$1,356,830.00 out of the deposit made of $3,148,500.00. There is no contest as well
that this sum of money belongs to GKL and was deposited to the account of PMCSL.
There is no contest that GKL is on solid ground in its claim for restitution. The contest
relates to whether PMCSL was an innocent recipient of these funds.
[18]
The parties also presented to the court and the court agreed that the sole issue to be
tried is
Whether PMCSL can defend this matter by proving that it
changed its position in good faith in dealing with monies
belonging to GKL.
PMCSL will successfully defend this case for restitution, if I am convinced that
PMCSL had changed its position in good faith. Two points therefore stand for
determination.
(1)
Was there a change in PMCSL’s position?
(2)
Was this change made in good faith?

[19]
EVIDENCE

(1)
GKL’S WITNESSES

STACY HENRIQUES

Page 6 of 33

Ms. Henriques testified that she was the Financial Controller of GKL. One facet of her
job was an in depth knowledge of the financial gains and losses of the Company. She
stated that she has full “control, custody and knowledge of all the financial books… and
access to all documents … I am ultimately responsible for all the financial operations…”.
Ms Henriques continued that if “there is a fraud perpetrated on GKL, the books,
documents and records concerning this fraud would fall within my control and custody,
and I would possess collective knowledge of same”. Ms Henriques then proceeded to
tell the court of GKL’s encounter with BM.
[20]
On September 14, 2005 BM presented GKL’s representative with the RBTT bank draft.
The draft was dated 9th September 2005, and made payable to Grace Kennedy (Trinidad
and Tobago) Limited, for the sum of US$500,000.00 drawn from the Bank of New York.
On the basis that the USD cheque was valid, Ms Henriques informed the court that GKL
issued written instructions to their Banker, Republic Bank Limited to issue a cheque in
favour of BM drawn on its account in the sum of $3,142,500.00. This was in purported
exchange for the USD cheque presented to GKL by BM.
[21]
Ms. Henriques stated that by letter of September 28, 2005 she was informed by
Republic Bank Limited, that the RBTT Bank Limited USD Managers’ cheque presented by
BM was fraudulent and further GKL’s account had been debited with the TTD equivalent
as per instructions. GKL issued a letter to RBTT Bank Limited requesting an enquiry into
the transaction, and the fraud was confirmed.
[22]
Ms. Henriques noted that upon investigation it was revealed that the cheque drawn
from Grace Kennedy’s Bank Account be disbursed as follows:
(a)
The issuance of Manager’s Cheque no. 12419516 in the name of
Bhola Maraj in the sum of $785,625.00;
(b)
The issuance of the Manager’s Cheque in the name of Bhola Maraj in
the sum of $571,205.00;

Page 7 of 33

(c)
The issuance of the Manager’s Cheque in the name of Ryen Singh in
the sum of $785,625.00; and
(d)
Cash in the sum of $1,000.000.00.
[23]
Investigations further revealed that the two cheques issued to BM were cancelled and
one cheque in the name of PMCSL in the sum of $1,356,830.00 was issued. These
transactions occurred on the 14th September 2005 at a time when GKL had no
knowledge of the true state of affairs and before GKL had obtained such knowledge of
“the fraudulent transaction”. PMCSL disbursed the proceeds of the cheque in the
following manner:
• FCB cheque made payable to Laurie Diaz Construction Company
Limited in the sum of $906, 830.00;
• FCB cheque made payable to Junior Thomas in the sum of
$60,000.00.
Ms Henriques testified that a Restraint Order of this Honourable Court is in place
freezing all of the proceeds of the fraudulent cheque in the sum of US$500,000.00 the
subject of the exchange of the GKL cheque in the TTD equivalent. This Order was
obtained pursuant to the PROCEEDS OF CRIME ACT 2000. Ms Henriques continues, “…
from PMCSL’s discovery documents, I note that the amount remaining in (PMCSL)’s
account at FCB as of 22nd June 2009 is $389,563.69.” Ms Henriques asks the court to
note that that the Restraint Order specifically identifies PMCSL as receiving the re-
negotiated cheque in the sum of $1,356,830.00 from BM which is admitted by PMCSL.
[24]
Ms Henriques was not cross-examined.
[25]
SARGEANT KESTER MC KAIN
Sgt. Mc Kain was at the relevant time attached to the Fraud Squad of the Trinidad and
Tobago Police Service. He had been so attached for a period of twenty (20) years. On or
about the 27th September, 2005, he was selected as the investigating officer into a

Page 8 of 33

complaint lodged by RBTT Bank. The investigation centered on GKL’s tendering for
payment a forged RBTT US dollar cheque in the sum of $500,000.00. He commenced
the process at GKL’s offices. Agt. Mc Kain confirmed the uncontested facts surrounding
the conclusion that BM was a fraudster. In the course of his investigations he
discovered that the manager’s cheque made in favour of “Ryen Singh” had been
destroyed. The funds were being held by Republic Bank in 2005. He learnt that on 19th
September, 2005 a cheque in the sum of $1,356,830.00 was deposited to the account of
PMCSL. He found out that on that day, PMCSL issued two cheques to Laurie Diaz
Construction Company Limited and to Junior Thomas for $906, 830.00 and 60,000.00
respectively. He further learnt that AB, AB was the Managing Director of PMCSL. He
interviewed AB at his office and learnt that he was “a consultant in construction” and
that “people would come (to his offices) to do photocopies and faxes”. Sgt. Mc Kain
stated: “The premises did have some office equipment but there was no evidence to me
that I could conclusively determine the extent of the business operations of (PMCSL).”1
[26]
THE PORTIA SINGH INTERVIEW
Sgt. Mc Kain testified that on 29th September 2005, he interviewed Portia Singh (PS) the
secretary of PMCSL. He learnt that she received a cheque from Junior Thomas in the
sum of $1,356,830.00 which she deposited to the FCB account held by PMCSL. Ms Singh
prepared cheques to be paid out to LDCCL and to Junior Thomas upon instructions from
AB. He recorded a written statement from Ms Singh which she signed. The information
contained in the statement mirrors that recited earlier in this judgment so I would not
repeat them here.
[27]
THE ALLAN BACHAN INTERVIEW
On 30th September he spoke directly to AB. He recorded a statement of the interview
which was admitted into evidence. AB confirmed to him that he left for Switzerland on
the 18th September, 2005 and left two pre-signed cheques with PMCSL’s secretary, Ms

1 See para. 17 of Sgt. Mc Kain’s Witness Statement filed November 02 2009.

Page 9 of 33

Portia Singh with instructions that on receipt of the cheque from BM that she was to
make two cheques payable to LDCCL in the sum of $906,830.00 and to Junior Thomas in
the sum of $60,000.00. Dr Bachan confirmed that he “knew Junior Thomas over one
year”.2 He was informed that Junior Thomas had a “client who was interested in
purchasing building steel and construction equipment”.3 Dr Bachan confirmed to Sgt.
Mc Kain that he met the client who he described as “an East Indian man”, sometime
around 14th September 2005. Sgt. Mc Kain drew the conclusion that this was BM.
Further discussions between the gentlemen are recorded as follows:
Dr Bachan informed me that he spoke to Laurie Diaz, who I later
learnt to be an individual also known as Laurie Andrews, and
informed him that Junior Thomas was interested in some steel and
construction equipment for his client. Dr Bachan informed me he
located some excess steel and some light equipment from Laurie Diaz
and this was conveyed to Junior Thomas.
Dr Bachan further expressly informed me that on/or about 14th
September 2005, BM sought to issue a personal cheque as payment
however, he Dr Bachan requested that he would only accept a bank
draft in relation to the above transaction and this was to be made
payable to this company and the copies of the identification of the
client be submitted to his office which (PMCSL) received on 19th
September 2005 from Junior Thomas.
[28]
ROLE OF LAURIE DIAZ CONSTRUCTION COMPANY LIMITED
Sgt. Mc Kain then went in search of LDCCL. He located Laurie Diaz who he took into
custody. Sgt. Mc Kain was taken to what he was informed was office accommodation

2 See para. 24 of Sgt. Mc Kain’s Witness Statement.
3 See para. 24 infra.

Page 10 of 33

but formed the view that “the room was not for his sole use and he seemed to be
passing through and merely using the facilities.”4 Sgt Mc Kain continued:
During this search, I observed a man who I recalled seeing at (PMCSL)
when I interviewed Ms Portia Singh and I requested his name he
informed me his name was Lindhurst Ishmael.
I know Laurie Diaz is a person who goes by the name of Laurie Andrews.
I am aware of this as a fact because, in or around 2005 there were
various proceedings pending against him relating to dishonoured
cheques in the Port of Spain Magistrates’ Court which is common
knowledge to members of the Fraud Squad.
At the time of investigation Laurie Diaz was arrested on suspicion of
fraud and was detained for one day; he assisted us with the criminal
investigation. He was released after a determination that at that time
there was not sufficient evidence to commit him5.
[29]
JUNIOR THOMAS

Sgt. Mc Kain had this to say in relation to Junior Thomas.
As an investigator at the Fraud Squad for over 20 years, Junior Thomas’
name is also well known to me. I am aware that he has been under
investigation and been a suspect in relation to various fraud matters.6
In relation to the three persons who he investigated, AB, Mr. Laurie Diaz and Mr. Junior
Thomas, Sgt Mc Kain testified as follows:
In the course of investigation and in my experience and time spent on
the Fraud Squad, I have concluded that Laurie Diaz, Junior Thomas and

4 See para. 27 of Sgt Mc Kain’s Witness Statement.
5 See paras. 28 -30 of Sgt Mc Kain’s Witness Statement.
6 See para. 32 of Sgt Mc Kain’s Witness Statement

Page 11 of 33

Allan Bachan are associates. By this I mean that they are connected to
each other and involved. I came to the view during the course of the
investigation that they were connected in relation to the facts as they
presented themselves and from the documents, the entire interplay
between the parties and the fact that Laurie Diaz and Junior Thomas
both have ties with PMCSL. 7
[30]
Sgt. Mc Kain confirmed that he sought and obtained a restraint order under Section 18
of the PROCEEDS OF CRIME ACT in relation to the forged USD cheque in the sum of
500,000.00. Sgt. Mc Kain confirmed that there was a balance in PMCSL’s FCB account
outside of the sums under the Order.
[31]
CROSS EXAMINATION
Of all Grace Kennedy’s witness, only Sgt Mc Kain was cross examined by Mr. Garcia.
This went to the information which he received to inform him that Dr. Bachan was in
Switzerland at the time of the deposit of the funds and his belief of that information.
Sgt Mc Kain stated that he had no reason to doubt that AB was out of the country but
agreed that it would have been “challenging” for AB to personally deposit the money at
First Citizens Bank Limited, Independence Square. He confirmed that the money was
actually deposited by Ms. Portia Singh.
[32]
Mr. Garcia requested clarification from Sgt Mc Kain of his statement in paragraph 33 of
his witness statement in which he “concluded that Laurie Diaz, Junior Thomas and Allan
Bachan are associates”. Sgt Mc Kain explained that he meant that they were “business

LAW
Both Counsel cited copious authority on the subject. I do not propose to examine all of
the authorities cited by them. The law is clear. As Lord Templeman states in LIPKIN
AND GORMAN: “the law imposes an obligation on the recipient of stolen money to pay
an equivalent sum to the victim if the recipient has been ‘unjustly enriched’ at the
expense of the true owner”.8 An innocent recipient of stolen money will be enriched if
he has not given valuable consideration for the money9. These are the unassailable
legal positions.

[56]
In equity, the position is expanded, as it were to ease the harshness of the law. Suffice
it to say that the starting point in analyzing this area of equity is and remains whether it
would be unjust or inequitable for a party to have restitution whether in whole, or in
part, if a defendant contends it would be unjust or inequitable or unconscionable “and
thus unjust”10 in all of the circumstances to ask him to make restitution since the monies
which he has received are no longer in his possession or control as he has parted with
them to another.11 He must go further to prove that such parting constituted a change
of position in good faith. It is now accepted that this defence is available to a
defendant.12
[57]
In this case, GKL has to demonstrate to the court that he must have the remedy. The
burden of proof is on it. It must come to the court making full and frank disclosure of all
the relevant circumstances. Above all it must come with clean hands. Once PMCSL is
relying on the defence, the burden falls on it to prove to the court that the change of
position was in good faith and that it is inequitable to ask it to make restitution whether
in full or in part.
[58]
A change of position is fairly easy to prove from the facts. In this case, it constituted
receiving money and parting with it to third parties. The issue to be examined is
whether this parting or change in position was in good faith. There is no one general
rule in deciding cases of this nature. Both the Privy Council and the House of Lords 13

the law, I have arrived at the following conclusions of fact:
1. That Bhola Maraj was a fraudster and he, Laurie Diaz, Laurie Diaz Construction
Company Limited, Lindhurst Ishmael and Junior Thomas were known to each other.
2. Lindhurst Ishmael, Dr Bachan’s business associate at PMCSL, was known to Bhola
Maraj, Laurie Diaz, Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited, Junior Thomas. He
was the common link between them and Dr Allan Bachan and PMCSL.
3. That Bhola Maraj, Laurie Diaz, Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited and Junior
Thomas engineered the plot to convert funds belonging to GKL.
4. That PMCSL was the conduit through which the funds were to be sanitized.

Page 27 of 33

5. That the Consulting and Retainer Agreement entered into by PMCSL and Laurie Diaz
Construction Company in January, 2005 was not actively operational since PMCSL
produced no evidence of income, expenses or profits to prove a course of dealings
between the parties.
6. That from the undisputed facts, GKL had parted with the monies on the faith that
the cheque presented by BM for negotiation was valid.
7. That the cheque presented for negotiation by BM was a forgery so that GKL’s funds
were converted by him.
Based on the above therefore, I find that GLK was entitled to seek restitution of the
funds paid to BM on the basis of the fraudulent cheque. I find as well that as a matter
of law, PMCSL could avail itself of the defence of change of position in good faith. The
burden of proof rests on PMCSL to prove all aspects of the defence.

[68]
I find as well that GKL’s carelessness or negligence in parting with its monies, the TTD
equivalent of US$500,000.00 is not to be taken into account in assessing whether it was
equitable to allow the claim for restitution in the face of the defence of change of
position in good faith when balancing its rights to restitution as against PMCSL’s defence
of change of position in good faith. The requirement of good faith on the part of PMCSL
is sufficient and I need go no further.
[69]
My findings continue as follows:
8. That the funds found their way into PMCSL’s account for onward transmission and
were transmitted to Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited and Junior Thomas,
ostensibly pursuant to the Consulting and Retainer Contract.
Because of this, it is crucial to examine the circumstances surrounding PMCSL’s receipt
of these funds from BM to determine whether PMCSL when it transmitted those funds
to Laurie Diaz Construction Company and Junior Thomas changed its position in good
faith.

Page 28 of 33

9. That PMCSL’s status at the time of the transaction whether experienced or fledgling
is immaterial to the question of good faith. By Dr Bachan’s evidence, it was a
company incorporated since 2002 and conducting business.
10. That there was a change in position is clear. PMCSL parted with $60,000.00 to Junior
Thomas and $906,830.00 to Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited.

[70]
In determining good faith, the linchpin of this case, all of the circumstances of the
change in position must be examined. There were many circumstances alluded to by
the parties, which are important in assessing whether PMCSL acted in good faith. I have
chosen the ones that I consider relevant for my deliberations. They are as follows:
a. The transaction, the subject matter of this action was the first of its kind for
what appears to be the Company’s only client LDCCL. That business with that
company commenced with this transaction, some nine months after the
Retainer and Consultancy Contract.
b. Interestingly, Dr. Bachan stated in cross-examination that he possessed a
“hands on approach” and was “very careful” and “precise”. This is
contradicted by his nonchalant conduct throughout the transaction. Dr.
Bachan claimed that PMCSL provided advice and ensured documents in place
for proper business transactions. If this were so, then why was he unaware
of Laurie Diaz Construction Company’s dealings and business history? His
lack of knowledge regarding the area of business in which Laurie Diaz
Construction Company was involved coupled with his lack of enquiry into the
only transaction conducted by Laurie Diaz Construction Company does not
carry his defence far.
c. The amount of money paid to Junior Thomas, $60,000.00 for messenger and
handy man services seem to be incompatible with his stated duties. There
was no evidence as to the period over which these duties were performed or
the rate of payment for the services rendered, the usual information

Page 29 of 33

associated with payments of this kind. It is remembered that he introduced
the parties at some point in time. Even if he served as the “business scout”
in this transaction, there is no evidence and quite sensibly so that the
payment had anything to do with this activity. For Dr Bachan not to have
asked a question or seek some kind of documentation for this transaction
belies his assertion that the change of position in this instance was in good
faith.
d. The quotation admitted into evidence as being prepared by Ms Portia Singh
on behalf of Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited, “PS1” was in the
sum of $1,218,431.00 and was unsigned and addressed to no one in
particular. That is not helpful in speaking to a course of business dealings in
furtherance of establishing the defence of change of position in good faith.

e. There is nothing tying the cheque which was prepared for Laurie Diaz
Construction Company Limited to the above quotation.

f. That the payment out to Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited for the
heavy machinery and equipment in the absence of accompanying invoices or
other supporting documents, raises suspicions and detracts from a finding of
change of position in good faith.

g. What is significant is Dr Bachan’s business sense and astuteness as seen in his
actions as principal of the company PMCSL. When BM asked if he could have
endorsed cheques in the Company’s favour, Dr Bachan refused and insisted
that the cheques which were to be made payable to the Company were to be
in the form of Manager’s cheques.
How then did Dr Bachan not question the bona fides of the transactions that he was
asked to participate in given his apparent knowledge of the dangers of receiving funds
of that magnitude from a cheque endorsed in his favour? In these modern times when

Page 30 of 33

commercial transactions are subject of heavy scrutiny I think it would have been
incumbent upon Dr Bachan to question the source of these funds from BM who he met
just prior to the transaction and with whom he claimed not to have a long relationship.
I conclude that Dr Bachan sought to protect his business while at the same time, turning
a blind eye to the transactions that PMSCL was asked to effect.

h. That Sgt. Mc Kain’s cross examination did nothing to alter his stated
conclusion of the nefarious relationship existing among the parties, Bhola
Maraj, Laurie Diaz, Junior Thomas, Lindhurst Ishmael and AB.
I am fortified in my wholehearted acceptance of Sgt. Mc Kain’s evidence of the
relationship between all of these parties to the fraudulent transaction and I accept his
conclusion as correct.

i. That neither Laurie Diaz nor Junior Thomas was called as witnesses for
PMCSL to verify their roles in the transaction or their relationships with
PMCSL.

[71]
I am of the view that GKL has made the case for the return of their moneys by PMCSL to
them. I am entitled to and in keeping with the dicta in MC QUEEN v GREAT WESTERN
RAILWAY COMPANY23 as cited by Rajnauth-Lee J in SIEUNARINE v DOC’S ENGINEERING
WORKS (1992) LIMITED, I draw adverse inferences from their non appearance as
witnesses and conclude that they would not have assisted PMCSL’s defence in this
matter by their recitation of the true circumstances of this case.

j. That there is no evidence of any bona fide, good or valuable consideration
passing between Laurie Diaz Construction Company Limited and PMCSL for
the service rendered of collection and disbursement of funds under the

23 (1875) L.R.10 Q.B. 569 and see p 10 of the SIEUNARINE CASE

Page 31 of 33

tainted transaction. There is no evidence that the sums retained represent
that consideration.
I can safely find that no good and valuable consideration exists and that the Consulting
and Retainer Agreement is a sham. Thus in all of the circumstances of this case PMCSL
cannot avail itself of the defence of change of position in good faith.

[72]
Even if I am incorrect on my interpretation of the facts and evidence that the
Consultancy and Retainer Contract is valid and not a sham, and the payments were
made in furtherance of their obligations under that contract,24 I find comfort in Lord
Goff’s dicta that if the correct position is that the parting with the funds to Laurie Diaz
Construction Company Limited and Junior Thomas was incurred by PMCSL in the
“ordinary course of things”, it is not inequitable in these circumstances to call upon
PMCSL to make restitution to GKL.

[73]
Mr. Kangaloo referred me to the FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS ACT 25 to make the point
that the Consultancy and Retainer Agreement violated its provisions in that under that
Agreement, PMCSL was contracted to “manage and disburse funds on behalf of” its
client. Mr. Kangaloo opined that this operation flies in the face of Section 5(1), in that
PMCSL had no licence to operate a “business of a financial nature” which included
“collection of funds in the form of deposits … and … the performance for reward of the
functions and duties of trustee”. He opines that:

In those circumstances by the second named Defendant collecting,
managing and disbursing monies on behalf of the Laurie Diaz
Construction Company, it is contended by the Claimant that such
management and disbursement of funds amounts to a collection of funds
in the form of a deposit and/or performance by the second Named

24 This is PMCSL’s pleaded case even though Dr Bachan first denied that the payments were made in
accordance with the Agreement on cross examination but later admitted that this was the case.
25 Chap. 79:09 repealed and replaced by the 2008 Act. The offences section is Sections 17(1) and (2) of
the 2008 Act.

Page 32 of 33

Defendant of acts of a trustee in relation to these funds of Laurie Diaz
Construction Company.
Should there be a violation of these sections, then PMCSL would face criminal sanction.
I take judicial notice that PMCSL did not have a licence to operate as a financial
institution but make no comment as to the effect of any apparent violation of this Act
on these proceedings.

[74]
On balancing the equities, GKL’s carelessness or negligence in parting with its monies,
the TTD equivalent of US$500,000.00 did not tilt the balance away from it. It is clear
that I can order PMCSL to repay the entire sum of $1,356,830.00 by way of restitution to
GKL in the terms to follow. The sums of $906,830.00 and $60,000.00 are be treated
differently from the sum of $390,000.00 (which the parties have agreed is due and
owing and did not form part of this deliberation) in terms of the interest and costs.
ORDER:
1. That there be judgment for the Claimant against the Second Defendant in the sum
of $1,356,830. 00.
2. That interest be paid on the said sum at the rate of 5.5% per annum from the 19th
September 2005 until the date of trial.
3. Thereafter, interest be paid on the sum of $966,830.00 at the rate of 5.5% from
the date of trial until the date of judgment and thereafter at the rate of 12% per
annum from the date of judgment to the date of payment.
4. That interest be paid on the sum of $389,563.00 at the rate of 8% per annum from
the date of trial to the date of payment.
5. That the costs be paid in the sum of $45,375.00 on the sum of $390,000.00 up to
the stage of the Pre-Trial Review as prescribed and in the sum of $94,341.00 on
the sum of $966,830.00 to trial as prescribed.

Page 33 of 33

6. That the payment of the said sum of $389,563.00 standing in the name of PMCSL
at First Citizens Bank standing in the Account No. 1084228 be paid to GKL after the
outcome of the proceedings CV 2005-06001.
I wish to place on record my gratitude to Counsel in this matter.

Dated this 28th day of July 2011.

/s/ CHARMAINE PEMBERTON
HIGH COURT JUDGE

title: LENNARD NELSON (Executor of The Estate of FREDERICK NELSON (DECEASED) v PATRICIA DE FREITAS (High Court, Trinidad and Tobago)
text:
Page 1 of 27

REPUBLIC OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE
CV 2008 – 02224
IN THE MATTER OF
THE ESTATE OF FREDERICK NELSON (DECEASED)
BETWEEN
LENNARD NELSON
(Executor of The Estate of FREDERICK NELSON (DECEASED)
Claimant
AND
PATRICIA DE FREITAS
Defendant

JUDGMENT
Before The Hon. Madam Justice Pemberton
Appearances:
For the Claimant:
Ms D Prowell instructed by Ms C Prowell
For the Defendant:
Mr C Gift S.C. instructed by Mrs J Gift

[1]
There are some housekeeping matters which I must address before I proceed to write this
judgment. The matters should have been addressed at the stage of the Pre Trial Review but since
the both Counsel made a request for an expedited hearing, I tried as hard as I could have to
facilitate them.

[2]
THE PLEADINGS
THE DEFENDANT’S DEFENCE
I recognize that the Defence bears close resemblance to Ms Patricia De Freitas’ witness
statement. Notwithstanding this, there are some paragraphs in the Defence which the court has
concerns about. Paragraph 18 contains facts which cannot be within this Defendant’s actual

Page 2 of 27

knowledge – hearsay - and in relation to which she would have difficulty leading this evidence at
trial. I have the same concern with that part of Paragraph 20 speaking to Frederick Nelson’s
seeking and obtaining permission from Harriet Nelson to construct a home and actually
constructing a home on a part or portion of the remaining land in the circumstances alluded to.

[3]
WITNESS STATEMENTS
Some parts of the Witness Statements presented contained hearsay and other forms of
inadmissible evidence which must be stuck out in order for a fair disposition of this case. I shall
examine the affected witness statement and record my findings.

[4]
THE CLAIMANT’S WITNESS STATEMENTS
LENNARD NELSON
Paragraph 6 line 3 and the words “the will as a beneficiary.” in line 4 are struck out as being
hearsay.
Paragraph 7 contains hearsay evidence and should have been expressed differently. I would
therefore make the following adjustments: Lines 2-3 delete the words “who was in that matter
asked that I bring it in for her to look at. I did. She advised that the will appeared to be
legally valid and”.

[5]
PATRICIA DE FREITAS
Paragraphs (2) to (8) of the Witness Statement of this witness filed on September 25th 2012 are
irrelevant and will not be considered for the purposes of this judgment.

Paragraph 10 cannot be classified as evidence in support of the facts surrounding this matter but
is, really a conclusion for the court to draw after considering the evidence as a whole. That
paragraph can be categorized as opinion as well and contains inaccurate statements and
assertions. If the testator’s intentions are contained in a will, the issues of paternity and proof
thereof do not arise. The paragraph is therefore stuck out and is to be disregarded.

Page 3 of 27

Paragraph 11 also contains conclusions which really ought to be drawn by the court and again is
an opinion on the nature of the matter expressed by the witness. This does not constitute evidence
of facts pleaded by the Defendant. The words on lines 2 – 3, starting at “and” up to the words
“still further” are to be disregarded. These words are to be struck out.

Paragraph 18 is struck out as this is hearsay. This witness has laid no foundation of her knowledge
of this state of affairs which does not involve her at all. The events predate her association with the
land in any material way. The most that this witness can say is that she resided at the original
family home with Harriet and Anastas Nelson, the children of Thomas and Catherine Nelson.

Paragraph 19, the words “without having abandoned same” are struck out and are to be
deleted. The witness is seeking to give evidence of another person’s intention. This is not
evidence that she can give without laying the proper foundation. Further, this is a conclusion to be
drawn by the court from the totality of the evidence.

Paragraph 21, the words “when he sought and obtained permission from Harriet Nelson …”
are struck out and are to be deleted. This witness cannot give evidence of this again without laying
a proper foundation. Was this witness present when permission was sought and given?

Paragraph 22, the words “was permitted by Harriet Nelson to erect …” are struck out and are to
be deleted. Again, no foundation was laid for this evidence.

Paragraph 24 the words “same was as a licencee” are to be struck out and are to be
disregarded. This is a finding to be made by the court after evidence of a relationship is led. Since
Paragraphs 19 and 21 are struck out, these words are struck out as well.

Paragraph 27 to my mind purports to give a legal conclusion on the merits of the case framed “in
the alternative”. The court is unsure of the purpose of this paragraph as it does not carry Ms
Patricia De Freitas’s case further and is unnecessary and irrelevant. This is the plea which should

Page 4 of 27

be in the pleadings. The witness statement is not the place to merely repeat the plea but to give
evidence in support of the plea. The paragraph is therefore struck out.

[6]
THE CLAIM – THE PROBATE ACTION
The Claimant, Mr. Lennard Nelson (“LN”) has had a long and fairly involved association with this
court over the subject parcel of land. He filed an initial action on 9th September 1999, which was
dismissed by this court. This fresh claim seeks the following relief:
1.
The court shall pronounce for the validity of the said last will and
testament of FREDERICK NELSON (deceased) in solemn form;
2.
Further or alternatively an order that probate of the said will be
granted to LN;
3.
A declaration that the Deed of Conveyance dated 29th day of
October 1976 and registered as 1908 of 1976 is null and void and of
no effect in so far as it purports to grant a fee simple interest in the
lands described therein to the Defendant;
4.
A declaration that the Defendant is not entitled to any share, estate
and or interest in the portion of lands described herein as the
deceased lands whether by way of possessory title or otherwise.

[7]
BACKGROUND AND UNCONTESTED FACTS
The lands, the subject matter of this action are situated in Calder Hall, Tobago. Those lands and
adjoining lands have been part of the Nelson family of Tobago for over a century. As is common in
Tobago, the family has been in occupation and I daresay undisturbed possession, but such
occupation and possession is not evidenced by any documentary title.

[8]
By his will, Thomas Nelson (TN) devised his lands to his children, “Susannah, Anastas, Frederick
(FN) Vivian, Harriet (HN), Amelia and any that may be born thereafter …”. TN’s will was admitted
to probate but there were no deeds of assent in favour of the beneficiaries. Upon the Grant of
Probate, there is some “official” recognition of the Nelsons’ “right” to the land by virtue of the
Assessment Roll of St. Andrew Parish in Tobago. In fact from an examination of the Extract, it

Page 5 of 27

appears that land taxes were paid for 2 roods for the period 1906-1908 under the name of the
owner “Thomas Nelson”. In the “Remarks” column, the words “Inherited from Paterson Nelson”
appear. Over the years the name of the Owner changed to Susannah, Frederick Nelson and
others and remained that way until 1996-2004, when presumably, the payment of taxes to that
office ceased.1 Suffice it to say that both Frederick and Harriet Nelson built structures on the land
and occupied these lands until their death which in the case of Harriet Nelson (HN) was in 1977
and Frederick Nelson (FN) was in 1980.

[9]
Before HN’s death, by Deed dated October 27th 1976 and registered as 19098 of 1976, (the 1976
Deed) she purported to divest herself of her rights in the entire parcel of land to her niece the
Defendant in this matter. PdeF then applied for and received a Certificate of Title for a part of
those lands measuring 10,857ft² the other portion is the subject matter of these proceedings. FN
died on July 17th 1980.

[10]
CLAIMANT’S CASE
As far as LN was concerned, his interest in the subject matter of these proceedings is born out of
his father’s will by which he was appointed the Sole Executor. On October 18th 2007, he made an
application for a Grant of Probate in Common Form of that Will. The description of the property to
be affected is as follows:
All that undivided piece or parcel of (land) and comprising One Rood or two lots more or
less and the hereditaments thereon being a two storey concrete dwelling house on the
northern portion of a larger parcel of land described all and singular that piece or parcel
of land situate at Morne Quiton in the Parish of St Andrew in the island of Tobago
comprising Two Roods and bounded on the North by lands of Elizabeth Nelson on the

1 The Extract revealed however that during the period 1963-1977, there was a material change to the records. The
Assessment number A-257 was allotted to the parcel of land but in the remarks column there is the notation “C/F
to XF-119”. Thereafter the Assessment number XF-119 still carried Susannah, Frederick Nelson and others as
owners but during the period 1978-1983 the remarks column reads “39.88 perches to Patricia de Freitas by R.P.O
Ret. #12/83 Vol 2753 Fol.7 C/F to ZZD-16”. Thereafter, from 1984-2004 the Assessment number XF-119 carried as
owners Susannah, Frederick Nelson and others with an acreage of 1 rood 0.12 perches. This was uncontradicted
so I take this as a true and correct position with respect to the lands under review by this court.

Page 6 of 27

South by lands of Caroline Graham on the East by a Road and on the West by a Public
Road and was assessed as A-257 but now Assessed as XF-119 in the Warden Office
in the Assessment Roll of St Andrew.

[11]
On December 20 2007, PdeF lodged a caveat against the Grant of Probate as a person having
interest in the said estate. On 20th March 2007 LN caused a warning to the caveat to be issued.
PdeF did not enter an appearance in the time limited and has to date caused no appearance to be
entered on her behalf.

[12]
LN filed this action asking for probate in solemn form as PdeF is not a blood relative of FN or a
person entitled on his intestacy and has no lawful interest in the grant of probate being made in his
favour.

[13]
THE DEFENDANT’S DEFENCE
The Defendant PdeF set up as part of her defence that LN slept on his rights, lachees, for which
she relied on the fact that shortly after FN’s passing in 1980, water and electricity connections were
severed and it was not until 19 years after the LN appeared to pursue any type of claim. PdeF
acknowledged that she brought only a portion of the land under the RPO and that was to meet her
financial needs at the time. PdeF avers that LN was not in possession of FN’s dwelling house in
1980 or at all and only made his presence known “in or about January 1999 consequent upon a
certain incident”. PdeF sets up her ownership of the entire parcel of land through the 1976 Deed
between herself and HN and reiterated the RPO process.

[14]
Further, PdeF avers that FN built a house on a portion of the land sometime in 1966, where he
lived until his death in 1980. PdeF stated as well that the monies came from the National Housing
Authority. PdeF continued that water and electricity were disconnected by the respective
authorities. PdeF then took exclusive control and possession of the said lands and remained there
until the incident in January 1999. She maintained that despite FN’s presence on the land she
maintained rights and control of the lands which continued on through 1983 when the land was
divided and a portion brought under the RPO.

Page 7 of 27

[15]
PdeF maintains that she does not know LN, never having seen him about or around the parcel of
land. It was on or about February 7th 1998, whilst passing near the land that she observed that
there were workmen in attendance at the house once occupied by FN. She then became aware
that LN had hired the workmen to effect repairs. She called a halt to the repairs.

[16]
It is noteworthy that PdeF did not directly address the Probate action in her defence.

[17]
EVIDENCE
WITNESS STATEMENTS – EVIDENCE IN CHIEF
CLAIMANT’S CASE
LENNARD NELSON
LN testified that he is a Retired Police Officer who lives in Trinidad. By this action he is asking the
court to pronounce on his father’s will (FN) in solemn form. LN stated that he was born in
Scarborough, Tobago to FN and Irene Joseph. He and his mother and sister lived together whilst
his father FN lived at Morne Quiton.

[18]
THE GRANT OF PROBATE
After FN’s demise, LN took his Will to his then attorney-at-law who proffered certain advice on its
validity. He accepted that advice. A certain incident took place which led him to seek further
advice. He had instructed his attorney-at-law to file an action on his behalf (“the first action”).
Whilst giving instructions, his attorney-at-law tendered certain advices which saw the filing and
prosecution of the matter at bar.

[19]
He recognized that none of the lands owned and/or possessed by FN had been transferred into
his, FN’s name. Those lands included those forming the subject matter of this action, the lands at
Calder Hall. Since the other dispositions in the will had been “distributed” to the named
beneficiaries, he included only these lands in his application for the grant of probate. He filed his
application on October 18th 2007. On December 20th 2007, PdeF lodged a caveat against the

Page 8 of 27

grant as a person claiming an interest therein. This caveat was warned on his behalf on March 20th
2008.

[20]
THE DECLARATION RE THE SUBJECT LANDS
LN testified further that he moved to live with his father at Morne Quiton in or around 1950 when a
fire destroyed the premises he shared with his mother and sister. At that time, FN lived in a
wooden house on the Northern side of a four lot parcel of land. A concrete house stands there
now. As far as he was aware, his Aunt Susannah Nelson was to have occupied the same spot – 2
lots with his father but she died on March 5th 1970 without having erected a house or living there.
His other two aunts, Harriet (HN) and Anastas lived on the other two lots in a boarded house. This
was on the southern end of the property about 45 to 50 feet from his father’s house. They later
renovated the house, replacing the boards with bricks. After Anastas died on September 28th 1973,
HN remained in sole occupation of that portion of the lands until her demise in 1977. PdeF is
Anastas’s granddaughter and she and her sister Pamela lived with their mother Suckie in the
house with HN.

[21]
LN testified that during FN’s lifetime, he identified the boundaries to him by showing him four iron
pickets. Hurricane Flora in 1963 left FN’s house in shambles causing him to move to his sister
Susannah’s house at Sergeant Cain. LN spoke to a meeting at that house on one of his visits. As
a result of these discussions, FN applied to the National Housing Authority for a loan to build a
“proper” house, on the understanding that he would have repaid the loan. The loan in the sum of
$5,000.00 was granted and he LN liquidated same in 1978. This was supported by receipts which
were accepted in evidence as agreed documents. Mr. Sydney Chevalier commenced the building
in 1966. When the upper portion was completed, FN moved there and lived there until his demise.
FN applied for and obtained water and electricity services which he maintained until his death.
Sometime thereafter, the lower portion was added and the two apartments were tenanted from
1970 until 1990. FN paid taxes for the half acre of land before PdeF’s title was entered and

Page 9 of 27

thereafter he paid building tax and land tax for the portion which he occupied. After FN’s death he
continued to pay the taxes.2

[22]
Upon FN’s death, LN took possession of his dwelling house and the portion of the lands and he
continued to exercise all rights of ownership as exercised by FN during his lifetime. He rented the
upper portion sometime after FN’s death. At some time he decided to effect repairs to the house
and the tenants moved out. In 1998, he contacted a building contractor, Mr. Dexter Campbell.
They visited the house after which he retained his services. Sometime after PdeF appeared and
ordered them off the premises. He tried to speak to her about her actions and she told him that
she put them out because they were trespassing on her property and to not speak to her about it
but to her lawyer instead.

[23]
LN spoke to PdeF’s then attorney-at-law Mr. Eric Taylor (now deceased) who provided him with
information re the 1976 Deed. He obtained a certified copy of the Deed and observed its contents.
His observations led him to the belief that HN was not the sole owner of the land. FN had survived
all of his siblings and was the last child of TN to die in 1980. He also made enquiries at the
Warden’s Office and observed that the number A 257 was given to the half acre parcel at Morne
Quiton.

[24]
He did further searches and came upon the Certificate of Title granted in connection with an RPO
application made by PdeF. He made further searches at the Warden’s Office and saw that this
parcel was given the Assessment number ZZD-16 and FN’s parcel was given the number XF-119.
He denied Pdef’s assertion that he was given any notice of any survey as she declared in her RPO
application. LN countered that he owns a house on that land that was occupied by tenants. His
half brother William Nancis collected rents on his behalf and neither was informed that any survey
was to take place on the lands. LN gave details of the RPO application and noted that PdeF
submitted the 1976 Deed in support of her application.

22 The receipts and evidence of payments were all received into evidence by agreement both as part of the Agreed
Documents and through various witnesses.

Page 10 of 27

[25]
CROSS EXAMINATION
LN was not shaken under cross examination. He confirmed his testimony in his witness statement
about his knowledge of his grandparents and the land, his relationship with his father, the fact that
his father left a will. He was not aware of any family home and that there may or may not have
been one. He knew that his father lived on the land and he knew where he lived before 1963 since
he was a regular visitor there. He knew of another house where HN and two other sisters lived.
His father owned and lived in a wooden house which was destroyed by Hurricane Flora. This
house stood on a half acre plot at Morne Quiton. The house that HN and her sisters occupied also
was at Morne Quiton. He maintained his ignorance of a family house on the land and staunchly
denied its existence. He confirmed that he knew that TN did not have a deed for the land he
disposed of by his will. He confirmed the history of the probate of that Will. He confirmed that he is
now in the process of obtaining a grant for FN’s Will.

[26]
He confirmed that he took FN’s Will to obtain legal representation for the purpose of obtaining a
grant of probate for that Will as he was concerned to get the title from FN to himself.

[27]

CAVEATS
In order to caveat any application, the caveator must have an interest to support the entry, for
instance, interest in the res, the subject matter of the application. I shall not rehearse submissions

obvious place, the Form which as authorized by the Rules “contemplates that the caveator should

caveator, whether it is an interest based on succession as opposed to a right to escheat. Further,
Wooding C.J. made reference to the warning to state that the interest must again be stated in the
warning so as to give it efficacy. It is important to note that this case deals with interests that need
to be stated and more than that, the nature of interests which can support a caveat and a warning.

LAW, ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSIONS
The deed was put into evidence. I found it a most interesting document and depicted a genre of
conveyancing that I do not recommend and which should be avoided at all costs. A close
examination of the Deed sees a Parties Clause describing HN as the Vendor and HN and PdeF as
the Purchasers; so far, so good. The Recitals in this document give some cause for disquiet. I
shall set them out in full. They are as follows:

WHEREAS the Vendor is seised in possession of the parcel of land
described in the schedule hereto for over twenty years.
AND WHEREAS the Vendor has contracted and agreed with the
Purchasers for the sale to them of the said land at and for the price or sum
of TWO THOUSAND SEVEN HUNDRED AND FIFTY DOLLARS.

[48]
This purports to show the Vendor’s title. First, I shall examine “seisin” from which the verb “seised”
is derived. Seisin describes the relation between a land holder and the land. One uses this
concept to describe holding the purest available form of land ownership, the fee simple, meaning
that it is capable of being inherited or disposed free of any condition, limitation or restriction on who

Page 17 of 27

can inherit or purchase. Seisin denotes formal legal ownership as opposed to mere possession or
a beneficial interest. A landowner therefore cannot be seised in possession. Put another way,
simply stating that the Vendor is “seised in possession” does NOT create a fee simple estate in
land. Including the twenty years for good measure does not assist. In any event, there is no recital
containing a description or a reference to a proper root of title, which if not mandatory is certainly
prudent for a deed to be characterized as a good deed. The interpretation to be placed on this
document therefore is that HN had no proper paper title to the lands described in the 1976 Deed.
Further, HN had no estate or interest to convey in the subject land. The classic principle is that
one cannot convey what one does not have. PdeF therefore acquired no estate, interest or benefit
from the 1976 Deed.

[49]
Further, if I agree with Counsel for PdeF’s submission as it relates to LN’s alleged share and
interest through his father then the same mutatis mutandis will apply to his client’s predecessor HN
and the same conclusion must stand in relation to PdeF. HN owned no fee simple estate. At the
date of that Deed, the estate remained unadministered and the property remained undivided so
that a one sixth share to which HN became entitled to under TN’s will was not identifiable. HN had
nothing but a floating interest in one sixth of the property which could not be transferred inter vivos.
Looked at from another standpoint, in 1976, there was one other surviving beneficiary of TN still
alive and well. HN passed away the year after, 1977 and FN in 1980, four years later. Could HN
deal with the entirety on her own in the way that she purported to do by the 1976 Deed? The
answer is obviously no.

[50]
There was nothing for HN to pass to PdeF. I find as a fact that the 1976 Deed was ineffective to
vest any estate or interest in PdeF.

[51]
CONVEYANCING AND LAW OF PROPERTY ACT Chap. 56:01.
Counsel for PdeF took comfort in Section 6(7) of the CONVEYANCING AND LAW OF
PROPERTY ACT Chap. 56:01. This provides a saving for “recitals, statements and descriptions of
facts and matters and parties” in deeds twenty years old at the date of the contract shall “unless
and except so far as they may be proved to be inaccurate be taken to be sufficient evidence of the

Page 18 of 27

truth of such facts and descriptions”. This section does not create rights, estates and interests
where none by law can exist. There is no estate or interest known to the law of Trinidad and
Tobago as being created by the words “seised in possession”. Further the addition of the words
“for twenty years” is not magical. No estate, interest or right described as such is known to our law,
notwithstanding possession for over twenty years. Further, the section operates as a slip rule to
save a deed, properly constituted and recognized by law from failure due to inaccurate statements
facts, matters and descriptions. The section does not give a life to a still born creature or an estate
or interest unknown to law. I have no hesitation in declaring that the 1976 Deed is invalid and
operated to transfer no estate or interest in PdeF.

[52]
CONCLUSION
I make the observation that PdeF has not provided any other evidence save the 1976 Deed that
could satisfy the requirement of the existence of her interest to give her locus standi to caveat LN’s
application for the Grant of Probate. From the foregoing analysis I find the 1976 Deed does not
assist PdeF in her quest. She cannot find her feet by the use of this Deed.
