[70]
It is not my intention to rehearse the evidence led but to analyse this claim in light of all that has
been above and the evidence led in this matter. In terms of PdeF’s possession or occupation of
the land, I find that that ceased once she physically moved from her aunt’s house as a young
woman, and during her aunt’s lifetime. Her aunt had no intention to claim against her siblings that
she had a right to be there on the basis that she had dispossessed anyone, least of all them. In
any event, the one who she could have claimed against, and the one against whom PdeF’s right
through her could have been asserted continued to live after her own demise. There is no

Page 25 of 27

evidence of any claim being made by HN against him, any evidence that she thought that her right
to be there was in any way superior to his, or moreover, any evidence that he thought that he had a
superior claim over the land which he abandoned and so one can claim that there was in him (FN)
sufficient animus to abandon and a concomitant sufficient animus in HN to dispossess him. The
issue of adverse possession simply does not arise in relation to these siblings. In terms of PdeF,
who was she going to dispossess if she was on the belief that the 1976 deed gave her legal
ownership? The answer is obviously no one. If I am wrong, what evidence has PdeF brought to
show that she exercised any rights of ownership over the land? Simply stopping repairs to the
existing structure which were commissioned by LN to my mind is not enough. That alone therefore
cannot constitute a sufficient act of ownership over the land.

[71]
PdeF has not in any way disputed the extract of the Assessment records. In fact PdeF admitted
that FN built a house with the assistance of the National Housing Authority, without attaching or
providing the court with any documents to support this fact. This was in fact corroborated by LN
who provided the records to show the relationship between the Authority and FN. PdeF stated that
FN paid water outgoings until his death and thereafter the tenants who were in occupation paid
them. She did not involve herself in that act. In fact this is not her pleaded case. She said in her
pleadings and reiterated in her witness statement that upon FN’s death the water and electricity
supplies were disconnected by the respective authorities on her initiation and that she took control
of the building and has maintained exclusive control and possession of same without let or
hindrance.

[72]
In fact, PdeF never disputed FN’s rights to be on the land during his lifetime. PdeF has brought no
evidence to show that she exercised any rights of ownership over the parcel of land for the 19
years before the first action was brought. Why wait until now to set up a case in Adverse
Possession over that portion of land, especially if she held the unwavering belief the 1976 deed
was “good”? This part of the counterclaim ought never to have been mounted. In actual fact, the
uncontested evidence of rentals being collected on behalf of LN up to 1990 belies any claim that
PdeF can sustain based on adverse possession.

Page 26 of 27

[73]
SHOULD THE AWARD OF COSTS READ “EACH PARTY BEARS HIS OWN COSTS OR
SHOULD COSTS BE AWARDED AGAINST THE DEFENDANT?
There was no fault evidential or otherwise with LN’s claim. LN’s claim stood fixed. There was
every need for PdeF to continue with her defence. Those are two of the differences between the
case at bar and the one before Gobin J. PdeF knew that she did not have a valid Deed in the 1976
deed. She knew or ought to have known that her evidence could not support her claim in adverse
possession. Why then did she first file the counterclaim and further, persist in it until this stage?

[74]
I have received no plausible explanations as to why the general rule ought not to be followed. The
evidence and analysis above clearly points to the inescapable conclusion that PdeF should pay to
LN the costs associated with her withdrawal of the Counterclaim at trial based on the Prescribed
Costs regime. I have therefore fixed the value of the Claim at $50,000.00 but will allow LN to
recover his costs in any event up to the Pre-Trial Review stage. That I believe shall meet the
justice of the case.

ORDER
ON THE COUNTERCLAIM
IT IS ORDERED AS FOLLOWS:
(1) That the Defendant Patricia de Freitas do pay to the Claimant Lennard Nelson costs
incurred as a result of the Defendant’s application for leave to discontinue same to be
assessed if not agreed.

ON THE CLAIM
IT IS NOW DECLARED AS FOLLOWS:
(2) THAT the Deed of Conveyance made between Harriet Nelson as Vendor of the One Part
and Harriet Nelson and Patricia de Freitas as Purchasers of the Other Part is null void
and of no effect in so far as it purports to grant a fee simple estate or interest in the
lands, the subject matter of this action.

Page 27 of 27

(3) THAT Patricia de Freitas is not entitled to any share, estate and/or interest in the portion
of the said lands, the subject matter of this action whether by way of possessory title or
otherwise.

(4) AND THE COURT PRONOUNCES for the force and validity of the last Will and Testament
dated 28th August 1978 of FREDERICK NELSON the deceased in this claim which is
referred to in the witness statement of the Claimant Mr Lennard Nelson a copy of which
is attached as “LN1” made herein the original of which is lodged in the Hall of Justice,
Port of Spain, Probate Department.

(5) AND IT IS ORDERED THAT Probate of the said original Will of FREDERICK NELSON be
granted to the Claimant LENNARD NELSON the Executor named therein.

(6) AND IT IS FURTHER ORDERED THAT the costs of this action be borne by the Defendant
Patricia de Freitas personally to be assessed if not agreed.

Dated this 25th day of April 2013.

/s/ CHARMAINE PEMBERTON
HIGH COURT JUDGE

title: HV HOLDINGS LIMITED v RAMRATEE HARRIPERSAD 1ST  ANDY SINGH 2ND  DECISION (High Court, Trinidad and Tobago)
text:
Page 1 of 10
REPUBLIC OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE
Claim No. C.V. 2009-03223

BETWEEN
HV HOLDINGS LIMITED
CLAIMANT
AND
RAMRATEE HARRIPERSAD
1ST DEFENDANT
ANDY SINGH
2ND DEFENDANT

DECISION

Before The Honourable Madam Justice Charmaine Pemberton
Appearances:
For the Claimant:
Mr. Seunath, S.C. instructed by Mr. Mohammed
For the Defendant:
Mr. Hansraj Bhola

[1]
FACTUAL BACKGROUND

The matter between the Claimant, HV Holdings Limited, and the Defendants,
Ramrattee Harripersad (RH) and Andy Singh (AS), revolves around the
possession of “All and Singular that parcel or lot of land known as Lot 97
Tarouba Road, Marabella”1. The facts are as follows:

1 Fixed Date Claim Form. Filed on Sept. 8, 2009.

Page 2 of 10
• Hubert Vincent Gopaul (HVG), owner of the lands prior to 1974,
tenanted the said lot to Kaiser Jagassar (KJ). (We have no information as
to when this tenancy commenced, but suffice it to say that it was
subsisting in 1971).
• On April 15, 1971, HVG served a Notice to Quit on KJ in the presence
of his daughter RH.
• KJ did not observe the Notice but continued to pay rent for the lands to
HVG, which was accepted.
• On February 20, 1974 by conveyance, HV Holdings Limited, Byron
Gopaul (BG) being a director thereof became the owner in fee simple of
the land.
• KJ died on May 30, 1986, leaving his wife Baboonie Kaiser (BK) in
possession of the property.
• BK died on December 20, 1996. RH remained in possession of the
property. (The relationship between BK and RH is not clear).
• RH continued to pay rent for the lands to HV Holdings Limited through
BG, until 2002 until his refusal to accept further rental payments.
• In or around January 2009, HV Holdings Limited through BG offered to
sell to RH the said lands at $150.00 per square foot.
• This offer was not acted upon. HV Holdings Limited now brings this
action to evict RH and her son AS.
• RH is claiming to have inherited a tenancy from her father KJ and
further, has now offered to pay half the market value for the said lands.

[2]
At the first Case Management Conference (CMC) in this matter Mr. Bhola,
Attorney-at-Law for RH questioned if the Fixed Date Claim Form filed on
September 8, 2009 disclosed a cause of action against his client. I ordered
submissions on this issue.

Page 3 of 10
[3]
DEFENDANT’S SUBMISSIONS

Mr. Bhola defended this action solely on the intention of the parties, in 1971. Mr.
Bhola submitted that the intention of the parties was that the tenancy continued
even after 1971 when the Notice to Quit was delivered, not acted upon but rent
was continually being paid and accepted. Those facts manifested that the tenancy
continued. Mr. Bhola submitted that as a result of HV’s acceptance of rent from
RH until 2002, that RH is a Statutory Tenant of the land under the LAND
TENANTS (SECURITY OF TENURE) ACT 1981. RH therefore had the
option of purchasing the said lands at half the market value. Mr. Bhola referred
me to several authorities on this point.2

[4]
Additionally, Mr. Bhola submitted that RH “has been in occupation of the said
lands for over Thirty Eight years (38 yrs) without any disruptions or interference
from anyone until now”3 and HV Holdings Limited is attempting to claim
possession of the lands simply because of RH’s disability and age.

[5]
CLAIMANT’S SUBMISSIONS

Mr. Seunath, Attorney-at-Law for HV Holdings Limited submitted that RH is
misguided in her conclusion that she is a Statutory Tenant. Mr. Seunath
submitted that after the service of the Notice to Quit, “Kaiser Jagassar remained
in possession under the provisions of the Rent Restriction Ordinance”4 deeming
KJ a Statutory Tenant. He relied on HILDA CYRUS V. EMMANUEL
GOPAUL5. That matter clearly states, “[t]he “statutory tenant” has no interest
in the land but merely a personal right to remain in occupation…it cannot be

2 SNELL’S Principles of Equity. 28th Ed. Chp. 5, pg. 556, sec. 2.
CENTRAL LONDON PROPERTY TRUST LTD. V. HIGH TREES HOUSE LTD. (1974) KB
COMBE V. COMBE [1951] 2 KB
FOSTER V. TROTMAN (1977) HC 2745. CRANE, J.
O’KIEFFE, CORRENE V. EMERY PETER AND SUSAN (1999) HC 1114. BEST, J.
3 Written Submissions and Authorities filed pursuant to the Order of the Honourable Justice Pemberton
made on the 30th October, 2009. Para 11.
4 Claimant’s Submissions. Para. 7(iii). Pg. 4. Filed on Dec. 18, 2009.
5 HILDA CYRUS V. EMMANUEL GOPAUL. (MAG. APP. NO. 69 OF 1987) PG. 7.

Page 4 of 10
transferred by the “statutory tenant” to another inter vivos, or pass under his
will, or vest in his legal personal representatives.”6

[6]
Mr. Seunath further argued that Section 15 of the ORDINANCE7 was applicable.
He contends that,
Section 15 of the [Ordinance] provides that no order or judgment
for the recovery of possession of any premises to which the
[Ordinance] applies, or for the ejectment of a tenant theref[ro]m,
shall be made or given unless one of the grounds set out in(a) to (r)
of the said section 14 is proved. Until the landlord is able to prove
one of those grounds, the tenant is entitled to remain in possession
under the terms and conditions of the original contractual tenancy,
but his status changes from that of a contractual tenant to that of a
tenant holding over under the provisions of the statute, and has
come to be called a statutory tenant.8
CYRUS also provides support for this point and states,
The expression “statutory tenancy” is a popular expression, first
used by Lord Coleridge J. in Hunt v Bliss (1919) 89 L.J.K.B. 174
at 177 to describe “the status of irremovability” acquired by a
tenant who continues in occupation under the Rent Restriction Act
after his contract of tenancy is determined.9
As such, Mr. Seunath submitted that RH is in fact a trespasser on the lands.

[7]
Mr. Seunath addressed the question of whether a new tenancy was created after
the Notice to Quit was served and rents continued to be paid and accepted. He
guided the court to several cases10 which demonstrate that unless there is a clear
agreement between landlord and tenant to create a new tenancy, then payment of

6 Id.

7 RENT RESTRICTION ORDINANCE. CHAP. 27 NO. 18.
8 Claimant’s Submissions. Para. 16. Pg. 8.
9 CYRUS at pg. 7.
10 DAVIES V. BRISTOW (1920) KB 428, 440 SHEARMAN, J.
ALI JUMANDEEN V. HV HOLDINGS LIMITED. CA NO. 93 OF 1998. DE LA BASTIDE,CJ.

Page 5 of 10
rent after a Notice to Quit, does not effectively do so. Mr. Seunath echoed the
utterings in DAVIES of Sherman J., who stated, “after the expiry of the notice to
quit the tenant is entitled to continue in occupation under the provisions of the
statute until those conditions arise which enable the judge in his discretion to
order recovery of possession or until the parties have arrived at a fresh
agreement.”11

[8]
Mr. Seunath further submitted that the dicta of de la Bastide, CJ in
JUMADEEN12 supported his view that neither RH nor AS are tenants of the
lands. Consequently, they do not fall under the protection of the LAND
TENANTS (SECURITY OF TENURE) ACT, 198113. Mr. Seunath dismissed
RH’s claim that she inherited a Statutory Tenancy from KJ and referred me to DE
HANEY V. ALI14.

[9]
In conclusion, Mr. Seunath submitted that RH’s defence did not have a realistic
prospect of success, and as a matter of course, I should conclude the matter at this
stage.

[10]
ANAYLSIS

1. Applicability of the Ordinance to the “Lands”
The determining statue in this matter is the ORDINANCE. This ORDINANCE
was in effect in 1971 when the Notice to Quit was served on KJ. Section 3(1)
states, “This Ordinance shall apply, subject to the provisions of sections 4 and 20
thereof, to all land which is building land at the commencement of this Ordinance
or becomes building lands thereafter...”15 There is contest that the disputed
premises are “building lands” within the ORDINANCE. Therefore, RH and
AS’s occupation of the lands fall within Section 3 of the ORDINACE.

11 DAVIES at pg. 441. This dicta agreed with that of HUNT V. BLISS [1919] W.N. 331.
12 JUMANDEEN at Pg. 10.
13 LAND TENANTS (SECURITY OF TENURE) ACT. ACT 11 OF 1981.
14 GERALDINE DE HANEY V. CYNTHIA GLORIS ALI. MAG. APP. NO. 169 OF 1984. MC
MILLAN, J.A.
15 RENT RESTRICTION ORDINANCE. SEC. 3(1)

Page 6 of 10
[11]
2. Tenant
Further, section 2 of the ORDINANCE defines “tenant” as including, “the widow
of a tenant who was residing with him at the time of his death…”16 Additionally,
this section goes on to state, “for the purposes of this Ordinance one letting of
premises shall be deemed to be in the same category as another letting of the
premises if both lettings are of – (a) building land; or…”17

[12]
Of particular importance in the definition of “tenant” is that provision is made for
only one transmission of the tenancy. In the instant matter, that tenancy was
transmitted to BK, the widow of KJ. Mc Millian J. in CYRUS further clarified
the position when he explained that the ORDINANCE does not provide for the
statutory tenancy forming part of the estate of the original deceased tenant. The
tenancy therefore can neither devolve to heirs nor be the subject of an inter vivos
transaction. Thus the statutory tenancy devolved to BK by virtue of her status as
JK’s widow. Upon BK’s death the statutory tenancy came to an end and reverted
to the reversioner – HV Holdings Limited.

[13]
3. Land Tenants (Security of Tenture) Act, 1981
The fatal flaw in Mr. Bhola’s defence is the fact that, as correctly submitted by
Mr. Seunath, RH and AS are not “tenants” of the lands. Therefore at the
operative date of the LAND TENANTS (SECURITY OF TENTURE) ACT,
1981 (the ACT 1981), they would have been unable to satisfy the “tenancy”
requirement in order to be covered by the ACT 198118. It stands to reason that
this ground of the defence also fails.

[14]
4. Continued Payment of Rent
A.
Rent Restriction Ordinance
Additionally, de la Bastide, CJ dispelled the misguided notion that because rent
was paid for an extended period of time that a new contractual tenancy was

16 Id. at sec 2.
17 Id.
18 LAND TENANTS (SECURITY OF TENURE) ACT. Sec 2.

Page 7 of 10
created. In JUMANDEEN he opined, “I would have thought that it was well
established law that the acceptance of rent per se from a person whose
contractual tenancy has been terminated, but who continues in possession under
the protection of Rent Restriction legislation, does not provide any basis for
inferring the creation of a new contractual tenancy.”19 This effectively dispels
Mr. Bhola’s argument that the extended period of time in which RH paid rent was
a reflection of the intention of HVG and later HV Holdings Limited and KJ.

[15]
B.
Common Law
Mr. Bhola provided an extract from “Yates and Hawkins” in an attempt to
support RH ‘s defence that the intention of the parties at the time of the receipt of
the Notice to Quit, must be determined. The passage reads, “landlords and
sometimes tenants, occasionally seek to “withdraw” a notice before the
operational date, or “waiver” its effect afterwards…A waiver may be deduced
from the parties’ behaviour…The question therefore is quo animo the rent was
received, and what the real intention of both parties was?...”20 I am not
convinced that this argument can hold in the case at bar.

[16]
CONCLUSION
Several factors affected the determination of this issue.
1. Applicability of the Ordinance to the “Lands”.
a. The premises in dispute at the time of original letting were subject to
the ORDINANCE.
b. Section 15 of the ORDINANCE conferred on KJ the status of
statutory tenant since none of the provisions had been satisfied for the
determination of the tenancy.
c. This conferred no interest in the land21.

19 JUMANDEEN at pg. 10.
20 Written Submissions and Authorities filed pursuant to the Order of the Honourable Justice Pemberton
made on the 30th October, 2009. Para 4. Filed on Jan. 13, 2010. This refers to the text Landlord and
Tenant Law. Yates, David and A.J. Hawkins. Pg. 257.
21 de la Bastide, C.J. states in JUMANDEEN at pg. 13, “a person who hold over under the protection of
the Rent Restriction law does so as a mere licensee who has no interest whatever in the land.”

Page 8 of 10
2. Tenancy
a. Upon KJ’s death, his tenancy was transmitted to his widow, BK.
b. Upon BK’s death, the statutory tenancy came to an end.
c. RH and AS did not qualify as “tenants” within the meaning of the
ORDINANCE.
d. The lands reverted to HV Holdings Limited, the fee simple owners.
3. Land Tenants (Security of Tenture) Act, 1981
a. Since BK became a protected tenant under the ORDINANCE, there
was no valid tenancy which could be protected under the ACT 1981.
b. RH and AS do not qualify as “tenants” covered by the ACT 1981
because at the operative date, June 1, 1981, BK was the recognized
statutory tenant under the ORDINANCE which did not provide for
further transmission after her death.
c. Consequently RH and AS receive no protection under the ACT 1981.
4. Continued Payment of Rent
a. The continual payment of rent to HV Holdings Limited and their
admitted acceptance until 2002 did not create a new contractual
tenancy between them.
b. Even if a new contractual tenancy had been created HV Holdings
Limited is still within its rights to seek to terminate it since only 6
years have elapsed since the date of the last acceptance of rent. The
limitation period has not expired.

[17]
In the face of these facts, it is clear that RH and AS have no realistic prospect of
success in this matter. Subsequently, under the provisions of Part 68 of the
CIVIL PROCEEDINGS RULES 1998 (CPR 1998)22, the requirements in Part

21 Part 68 of the CPR 1998 states,
68.3 The claimant must file with the claim form evidence stating -

(a)
his interest in the land;

(b)
the circumstances in which the land has been occupied
without licence or consent;

22 Part 68 of the CPR 1998 states,

Page 9 of 10
68.3 are satisfied by HV Holdings Limited. HV Holdings Limited submitted
evidence which,
• showed their interest in the disputed lands,
• explained the circumstances in which the land was occupied without license or
consent, and
• the circumstances in which the claim to possession arose.23

[18]
Therefore, pursuant to Part 68.7(1) summary judgment may be entered for the
Claimant.

DECISION:

1.
That Fixed Date Claim Form filed on September 8, 2009 does reveal a
cause of action against the Defendant.

2.
That the Defendant’s defence does not present a realistic prospect of
success.

68.3
The claimant must file with the claim form evidence stating -

(a)
his interest in the land;

(b)
the circumstances in which the land has been occupied
without licence or consent;

(c)
the circumstances in which his claim to possession arises;

(d)
that he does not know the name of any person occupying the
land who is not named in the claim form; and

(e)
full particulars of the efforts he has taken to identify any
person occupying the land who is not named in the claim
form.
…
Powers of court at first hearing.
68.7

(1)
At the first hearing the general rule is that the court must
give judgment unless there is a defendant attends and
satisfies the court that he has a defence with a realistic
prospect of success.

(2)
…
23 Claimant’s Submission. Para. 4. Pg. 2

Page 10 of 10
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED AS FOLLOWS:

1. That Summary Judgment be given in favour of the Claimant.

2. That the Defendant do pay the Claimant’s costs to be assessed.

3. Claimant to file and serve Statement of Costs on or before March 25, 2011.

4. Defendant may respond on or before April 15, 2011.

5. Date of Assessment May 13, 2011 at 10:45am in SF02.

Dated this 18th day of February 2011.

/s/ CHARMAINE PEMBERTON
HIGH COURT JUDGE

title: MARK BARTLETT 1st  HEIDI BARTLETT 2nd  MICHAEL MURPHY 3rd v THE DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTION 1st  THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO 2nd  *********************** (High Court, Trinidad and Tobago)
text:
Page 1 of 8
REPUBLIC OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO

IN THE HIGH COURT OF JUSTICE

CV2010-00838

BETWEEN

MARK BARTLETT
1st Claimant

HEIDI BARTLETT
2nd Claimant

MICHAEL MURPHY
3rd Claimant

And

THE DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC PROSECUTION
1st Defendant

THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
2nd Defendant
***********************
Before Hon. Madame Justice C. Pemberton

Appearances:
For the Claimant:
Mr. A. Razack
For the Defendant:
Ms. R. Hosein

JUDGMENT

[1]
On May 7, 2008, Mark Bartlett, Heidi Bartlett and Michael Murphy were all
charged with offences under section 49 of the Summary Offences Act.1
They were all placed before a Magistrate after being formerly charged.
The matter came up for hearing in February 2010 and was adjourned.
During the hearing, it is alleged that the Attorney for the parties indicated

1 Id. at 3.

Page 2 of 8
to the learned Magistrate that he was prepared to “seek a ruling on the
points of law raised in regards to disclosure”.2

[2]
It is further alleged that, “The Magistrate subsequently adjourned my (his)
matter to the 8th of March 2010, and stated, ‘that she was tired of hearing
these applications for disclosure and wanted to proceed to trial'.”3

[3]
Based on these statements, the parties entertained certain fears as stated
hereunder:

“that by proceeding to trial without the issue of disclosure
properly being dealt with and not having the benefit of the
Magistrate hear legal arguments as requested by my
Attorneys at Law, that my Constitutional right to a fair trial
and disclosure of information in the possession of the
state, will be breached.”4

[4]
By Fixed Date Claim Form, the Claimants approached the Court seeking
the following constitutional relief:

(a)
A declaration that the right of the Claimants to
liberty, security of person, and enjoyment of property are
and not to be deprived thereof, except by due process of
law and the right guaranteed to each of them by section
4(a) and (b) of the Constitution of the Republic of
Trinidad and Tobago as further particularized in section
5(2)(e),(f)(ii) and (h) thereof have been, are being or is
likely to be contravened in relation to each of them, by
the failure of the State Authorities to provide each of

2 Id. at para 10.
3 Affidavit of Mark Bartlett. Filed Mar 5, 2010. Para 11.
4 Id. at para. 12

Page 3 of 8
them in advance with any material of which the State
Authorities are aware which would tend either to
materially weaken the State’s case or materially
strengthen the case for the Defence in the criminal trial
against the Claimants arising out of Magisterial No:
3567/08, 3566/08, 3565/08 (hereafter referred to as “the
said proceedings”).

(b)
An
order
directing
the
Director
of
Public
Prosecutions to disclose and/or cause to have disclosed to
the Claimants the said materials in advance of the
commencement of the trial of the said proceedings.

(c)
Consequent upon (b) above, an order staying the
said proceedings against the Claimants pending the
disclosure of the said materials as required by (b) above.

(d)
An order directing the Magistrate seized of the said
proceedings to hear and determine according to the law, in
the event that the parties are unable to agree, the said
materials.5

On April 28, 2010, at the CMC, they all professed their innocence.

[5]
Having perused the papers, I formed the view that there was a preliminary
issue arising in this matter. I framed it as, “Based on the facts
presented, can the reliefs claimed on the Originating Motion be
entertained in a Constitutional Court?” The parties filed written
submissions
and
the
Claimants
responded
to
the
Defendants’
submissions. I shall only state the salient features of their submissions.

5 Originating Motion. Filed Mar 5, 2010. pg. 2-3.

Page 4 of 8
[6]
THE ATTORNEY GENERAL AND THE DIRECTOR OF PUBLIC
PROSECUTION

The crux of the Defendant’s submissions is that this is an abuse of the
court’s constitutional jurisdiction, since there was an alternative remedy.
The Claimants’ proper remedy lay in judicial review of the Magistrate’s
decision. Counsel submitted further that, “[t]he pleadings on the face do
not disclose any breach of a constitutional right. A mere allegation of a
breach of a constitutional right will not suffice to successfully invoke
proceedings under section 14(1) of the Constitution.”6 The Defendants’
placed reliance on sections 3, 5(1), 5(2) and 15 of the JUDICIAL REVIEW
ACT7 and a slew of well known and recognized authorities8.

[7]
THE CLAIMANTS’ SUBMISSIONS

In response, Mr. Razack informed the Court that three issues were raised
for consideration. These issues were, the constitutional duty of the
Director of Public Prosecutions, the duty of the Director of Public
Prosecutions and the alternative action to be taken if the Court believes
that constitutional relief is inappropriate. Mr. Razack then launched into a
foray on these issues.

[8]
Mr. Razack further filed what he termed a reply to the Defendant’s
submissions, in which he identified the constitutional duty of the Director of
Public Prosecutions. This was “to conduct litigation as a minister of justice
which includes:

6 Full Written Submissions on Behalf of the Defendant. Filed Jun 30, 2010. Para. 4.
7 JUDICIAL REVIEW ACT, 2000.
8 THE ATTORNEY GENERAL FOR GAMBIA V. JOBE (1984) AC 689 AT 700; MATTADEEN V.
POINTU, 1999 AC 98; THAKUR PERSAD JAROO [PRIVY COUNCIL 54 OF 2000];
MAHARAJ V. THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO (1979) AC 385, AT
395 F-G; THE MAYOR, ALDERMAN AND BURGESSES OF SAN FERNANDO V.
CHANDRAWATEE RAMLOGAN CIVIL APPEAL NO. 54 OF 1985; HARRIKISSOON V. THE
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO [1984] 1 ALL E.R. 694; THE
ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO V. GEORGE JOSEPH. CIVIL
APPEAL NO. 63 OF 2002; THE ATTORNEY GENERAL OF TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO V.
DURHAM MCLEAN. CIVIL APPEAL NO. 74 OF 2002.

Page 5 of 8
•
Obedience to the rights of the accused person/s to a fair trial
as guaranteed by the Constitution of Trinidad and Tobago;9
•
That the Director of Public Prosecutions as a Constitutional
Officer is under a positive duty to provide statements of
witnesses;10

[9]
Mr. Razack then, through his submissions, “sought the Court’s guidance
on the duty of the Director of Public Prosecutions to ensure that all
persons accused in criminal matters can receive a fair trial as guaranteed
by the Constitution of Trinidad and Tobago.”11 To his mind, “[t]hese rights
include, [t]he right to disclosure and such fundamental rights given by the
Constitution.”12 Further, “[u]nder the provisions of the Constitution, there
are no other procedures to be taken against the Director of Public
Prosecutions for breach of Constitutional duties.”13 In Counsel’s opinion,
“[t]his matter necessarily involves an interpretation of constitutional
provisions, the right to a fair trial and the rule of law. A magisterial court
has no jurisdiction to determine or consider statutory provisions or rule of
law.”14

[10]
Counsel continued:

“Further and in the alternative, should this Court be of the view that a
Constitutional Motion and/or Constitutional relief not be appropriate,
the Court should set a timetable and give directions for the matter to be
dealt with, as it has become evident that in the absence of directions, it

9 See Seeromanie Maraj-Naraynsingh v the Director of Public Prosecutions (unreported) C.A. Civ. 33
[2007] and Dhanraj Singh v The Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago and the Director of
Public Prosecutions H.C.S. S395 [2001], H.C.S. 474 [2001].
10 See Jasper v United Kingdom [2000] 30 EHRR 441, HM v McInnes [2010] UKSC 7, HM v
Murtaugh [2009] PCA 11.)
11 Claimant’s Reply to Defendants’ Written Submissions. Filed Jul. 30, 2010.
12 Id.
13 Id. See Minister of Home Affairs v Fisher [1979] 3 All ER 21 at pg 21, at page 26, letters D and E and
page 25, letter h.
14 See ex parte Bennett [1994] 1 AC 42.

Page 6 of 8
will not be possible for the Claimants to receive a fair trial as
guaranteed by the Constitution.”15

ANALYSIS AND CONCLUSION
[11]
I considered the submissions carefully. Mr. Razack did not treat with the
preliminary issue raised but sought to introduce through his submissions
an entirely different case from the one at bar. The submissions bore no
relevance to the factual matrix upon which the reliefs which were claimed
or for that matter, did they address the preliminary issue which was under
consideration. The Defendants’ submissions offered more assistance and
stated fundamental positions in law. Mr Razack’s submissions did not
meet with my favour at all.

[12]
My own view of the matter can be summarised as follows:

1) There is no allegation of any breach of any constitutional right on the
case as pleaded so that the Constitutional jurisdiction of the Court cannot
be invoked;

2) There is no allegation of any untoward behaviour or dealings by the
Director of Public Prosecution on the case as pleaded;

3) The matter is still alive and is engaging the attention of the learned
Magistrate. It was adjourned, not dismissed, so that the learned
Magistrate’s alleged utterances cannot, and in fact, did not amount to a
rejection of Counsel’s stated “indication” that he was prepared to make
certain submissions to the Court. I use the word alleged since there is no
corroborating or confirmatory evidence that these indeed were the words
used by the Magistrate.

15 see Attorney General of Trinidad and Tobago v Ramanoop [2006] 1 AC 328 at page 328, paragraph
30.

Page 7 of 8

4) Even if I were to find that the decision of the Magistrate was
reviewable, and that is not the case before me, and an adjournment in the
way stated and in those alleged circumstances is not commensurate with
a definitive position or a decision capable of being reviewed.

5) This action is premature.

[13]
I may add that one must not use the constitutional jurisdiction of the court
to advance positions which must necessarily engage the Magistrate’s
attention. It is tantamount to enlisting the High Court to usurp the powers
of the magistrate conferred by the Statute16. Further, one does not invoke
the court’s jurisdiction to seek guidance. There must be a factual matrix
speaking to infringement of fundamental rights for the court to be moved.
Anything else amounts to an abuse of process, which this action has
proven to be.

[14]
In the premises the reliefs claimed on the originating motion cannot be
entertained by a constitutional court at this stage. Having come to that
conclusion, I am left with no option but to dismiss the motion filed and
order that the Claimants pay the Defendants’ costs in the usual manner.

IT IS HEREBY ORDERED AS FOLLOWS:

1.
The Fixed Date Claim Form filed on March 5, 2010 be and is
hereby dismissed with costs to be paid by the Claimant’s to the
Defendants’.

2.
Defendants’ are to file and serve their Statement of Costs on or
before October 29, 2010.

16 Disclosure is an issue to be dealt with by the Magistrate at that stage of the proceedings. Further a Stay
of Proceedings will only be granted in certain specified conditions. Those have not been met in this
action.

Page 8 of 8

3.
Assessment of costs to take place on December 13, 2010 at 11:00
am, SF02.

Dated this 30th day of September, 2010

Charmaine Pemberton
High Court Judge

BACKGROUND
The Claimant, Ms. Neutrice Greaves, is the aunt of the Defendant, Ms.
Nina Grant. On February 23, 1020, Ms. Greaves, weary of requesting that
Ms. Grant vacate the property “situate at and known as No. 195
Dundonald Hill, Long Circular, Maraval, St. James”1, filed an action to
effect same. Ms. Grant filed her Defence on April 12, 20102.

2 Defence , filed on Apr. 12, 2010.

On April 13, 2010, the date of the first Case Management Conference
(CMC), the parties were referred to community mediation. At the third
CMC on October 4, 2010, Mr. Pope, Attorney at Law for Ms. Grant,
informed the Court that no efforts for mediation were made by the parties.
Neither Ms. Greaves nor her then Attorney at Law, Mr. Scobie, appeared
in Court on that occasion. On July 12, 2011, at the fifth CMC Ms.
Greaves with her new Attorney at Law, Mr. Scotland appeared before the
Court and parties were again ordered to mediation for resolution of the
matter. It was not until the eighth CMC on February 1, 2012 that the

complied with. The parties had reached an agreement in principle before
the Mediator at Community Mediation. A tentative agreement between the
parties failed to fully satisfy Ms. Grant.3

On February 1, 2012 it was ordered as follows:

1. Witness Statements to be filed and exchanged on or
before the 20th day of April 2012.
2. Witness Statements to stand as Examination in Chief.
Cross –Examination only at Trial. 4.

Ms. Greaves’s witness statement was filed on April 11, 2012. Ms. Grant’s
witness statement however was filed on May 17, 2012, 27 days past the
filing deadline, and there was no timely application for relief from sanctions
forthcoming in this regard. Consequently, Ms. Grant was not permitted to
lead evidence at the trial. The trial commenced on July 10, 2012.

[4]
PLEADINGS
Claimant’s Statement of Case
Ms. Greaves claims that she is entitled to possession of the entirety of,

ALL THAT three bedroom concrete dwelling house standing
on a parcel of lands owned formerly by the heirs of J. Sabga,
now the State, situate at and known as No. 195 Dundonald
Hill, Long Circular, Maraval, St. James which said parcel of
land is bounded on the East and West by lands formerly or
now of Sabga, on the South by Dundonald Hill and on the
North by a Road Reserve, together with the tenancy rights to
the said parcel of land (hereinafter called “the said property”).
The said property contains a two bed roomed concrete
dwelling house which is now occupied by the defendant,
Nina Grant. This two bed roomed apartment is hereinafter
referred to as “the said downstairs”. 5

It is undisputed that on January 24, 2005 the subject property was
transferred to Ms. Greaves by way of Deed of Assent from the estate of
Juanita Reid, her mother.6 Ms. Greaves claims that Ms. Grant was given
permission to occupy a portion of the property from Ms. Brown, who was
Ms. Grant’s mother and Ms. Greaves’s sister. Ms. Greaves states:

7.
During the lifetime of the deceased Juanita Reid, one
Mildred Brown, the claimant’s sister gave the
defendant permission to occupy the said downstairs.
Mildred Brown died before Juanita Reid. The said
Mildred Brown was never the owner of the said
property or any part of it, nor was she ever authorized

5 Statement of Case filed on Feb. 23, 2010. Para 1.
6 Id. at para. 4.

by Mildred Brown to permit the defendant to occupy
the said property.

8.
Since the death of Mildred Brown and the claimant’s
ownership of the said property, the defendant has
been waging a campaign of harassment and threats
against the claimant’s tenant and has denied that the
claimant is the owner of the said property.

9.
The defendant is neither the tenant nor the licensee of
the claimant and neither the deceased Juanita Reid
nor her predecessors nor successors in title have ever
consented to the occupation of the said downstairs by
the defendant. The defendant is unlawfully in
possession of the said premises.7

As such, Ms. Greaves prays for possession of the property, damages in
trespass and costs.8

[5]
Defendant’s Defence
Ms. Grant defended her right to occupy the property and claims that she
inherited this right through Mr. Herman Reid. She states:

After the death of JUANITA REID (the Deceased) however,
under the provisions of the Administration of Estates
Ordinance, Chapter 8:01, the legal right to the property
should have passed to HERMAN REID, now deceased, as
next-of-kin, the late husband of the Deceased – they were
married to each other on 15th April, 1985...Accordingly, the

7 Id. at paras. 7-9.
8 Id.

Page 5 of 17
legal claim of the Claimant, under the provisions of the
Distribution of Estates Act Number 28 of 1998, amounted
only to ½ undivided share of the property.9

[6]
In addition to her claim that Ms. Greaves is not entitled to occupation and
possession of the entire subject property, Ms. Grant also claims that Ms.
Greaves was unscrupulous and perpetrated a fraud during her
administration of the estate of Ms. Juanita Reid. In her Defence Ms. Grant
stated:

The Defendant admits to occupying the ground floor
apartment referred to in paragraph 6, but avers, however,
that the Deceased herself (who was her grandmother) and
her then husband, HERMAN REID, deceased, before their
deaths, gave tacit approval to her occupancy of the
apartment. Moreover, MILDRED BROWN, now deceased,
who was the daughter of the Deceased and sister of the
Claimant, gave her approval also. The said MILDRED
BROWN, deceased, was the sole appointed executrix of the
will of the Deceased, published on the 29th March,
1978...And it is interested to note that the Defendant was 1
of the 3 named beneficiaries to whom the Deceased at death
had given her said property after the demise of her husband,
HERMAN REID, who was given a life interest. From an
endorsement on the said copy of the will of the Deceased,
the Claimant herself acknowledged accepting delivery of the
original copy of the said will on the 7th March, 2003, but in
her haste “to administer” the estate of the Deceased,

9 The Defendant’s Defence, filed Apr. 12, 2010. Para. 2.

Page 6 of 17
selfishly and fraudently (emphasis mine) thought it best to
withhold information as to its existence.10

[7]
EVIDENCE
Claimant’s Evidence

Ms. Greaves attested that she obtained the Letters of Administration for
her mother on November 5, 2004 and subsequently received the Deed of
Assent to the subject property on January 24, 200511. She informed the
Court that since her mother’s death she has occupied the upstairs portion
of the property and currently rents the same to Ms. Lorna Boodoo.12 In
addition to presenting the Court with the Deed of Assent, Ms. Greaves
noted that contrary to Ms. Grant’s claim that she was a tenant of the
property, that she was the owner as evidenced by the last receipt showing
that she pays the Land and Building Taxes for the property.13

[8]
Cross Examination of Ms. Greaves

In cross examination Ms. Greaves confirmed the evidence contained in
her witness statement. She stated that Ms. Grant was her sister’s
granddaughter and noted that Ms. Grant came to live on the property
while Mrs. Juanita Reid was still alive, as she was sent to take care of Mr.
Herman Reid. Ms. Greaves also agreed that Mr. Herman Reid shared the
property with her mother before her death, but he was not related to her
or her sister, Ms. Brown.

[9]
The Court also asked additional questions of Ms. Greaves in an attempt to
paint a complete picture of the matter. When questioned regarding the
existence a will as claimed by the Defendant, Ms. Greaves admitted
knowledge of same but stated that Mildred Brown, Ms. Grant’s mother,

10 Id. at para. 6.
11 Witness Statement of Neutrice Greaves, filed on Apr. 11, 2012. Paras. 7-8 .
12 Id. at para. 10.
13 Id. at para. 9.

Page 7 of 17
pre-deceased Ms. Juanita Jordan Reid. In any event, the will spoke to
Juanita Jordan and that person subsequently married Mr. Herman Reid in
1985.

[10]
Defendant’s Evidence

Ms. Grant was not permitted to lead evidence because her witness
statement was filed outside of the time stipulated by the Court.14

[11]
SUBMISSIONS
Claimant’s Submissions

Mr. Scotland submitted that Ms. Greaves is entitled to exclusive
possession of the subject property. He submitted that Ms. Grant’s
Defence fails
to
comply
with
the
requirements of
the
CIVIL
PROCEEDINGS RULES, 1998 (CPR 1998) Part 10.5, and emphasized
that the Defence did not fulfil the requirements of Parts 10.5(3) and
10.5(4).15 Mr. Scotland submitted that:

After consideration of the authorities, the unavoidable realty
is that the Defence in this case fails to comply with the
requirements set out in Part 10.5 of the CPR. The
Defendant in paragraph 1 of its Defence gave a base denial
to the assertion that the Claimant is the legal owner of the

14 See Decision of July 10, 2012, in which the Defendant’s witness statement was disallowed.
15 Part 10.5(3) and (4) states:
(3)
In his defence the defendant must say -
(a)
which (if any) allegations in the claim form or statement of case he admits; and
(b)
which (if any) he denies; and
(c)
which (if any) he neither admits nor denies, because he does not know whether
they are true, but which he wishes the claimant to prove.
(4)
Where the defendant denies any of the allegations in the claim form or statement of case-
(a)
he must state his reasons for doing so; and
(b)
if he intends to prove a different version of events from that given
by the claimant, he must state his own version.

Page 8 of 17
property
without
providing
any
grounds/reasons
for
challenging the claim.16

Based on the filed Defence, Mr. Scotland felt justified in making his
application for the Defence to be struck out. Highlighting the fact that no
reasons were given in the denial of the claim, Mr. Scotland referred the
Court to several cases on this point. The cases of note include M.I. 5
INVESTIGATIONS LTD. V. CENTURION PROTECTIVE AGENCY
LIMITED17 and ANDRE MARCHONG V. TRINIDAD AND TOBAGO
ELECTRICITY
COMMISSION
AND
GALT
AND
LITTLEPAGE
LIMITED18.

[12]
M.I. 5 INVESTIGATIONS addressed an appeal form the striking out of a
defence because it revealed no defence, thus failing to comply with Part
10.5. In that matter, the Honourable Mr. Justice of Appeal Mendonca
mused that when an Appellant is in violation of Part 10 of the CPR 1998
“the Court is entitled to treat the allegation in the claim form or statement
of case as undisputed or the defence as containing no reasonable
defence to the allegation.” 19 Mr. Scotland submitted that this approach is
applicable in the instant matter and the Court should treat the Statement
of Case as undisputed20.

[13]
In ANDRE MARCHONG, the Honourable Madame Justice Jones
reiterated the validity of Part 10.5 and its application in the M.I. 5
INVESTIGATIONS21. The learned judge mused that the rule:

16 Claimant’s Submission. Para. 17.
17 Civ Appeal No. 244 of 2008.
18 H.C. 4045/2008.
19 M.I. 5 INVESTIGATIONS LTD. at para. 10.
20 Claimant’s Submissions. Para. 19.
21 ANDRE MARCHONG at para. 11.

Page 9 of 17
Accords with the policy of full disclosure and an avoidance of
litigation on issues which are unnecessary and a waste of
resources22.

Consequently, and in the absence of any other provisions, the learned
judge surmised that:

In our jurisdiction a defendant must plead to every allegation
made against it and confirm its plea by the required
verification. It follows that, with respect to liability and
damages equally, a defendant cannot put a party to proof
without complying with part 10.5(3)(c). In accordance with
the MI5 Investigations case a failure to comply with the rule
entitles the court to treat the allegations as undisputed.23

[14]
Additionally, Mr. Scotland noted that Ms. Grant’s locus standi is not
pleaded. He concluded that because she is not a blood relative “she is
not entitled to any interest in his (Mr. Herman Reid’s) estate if he has
any”.24 He highlighted that Ms. Grant presented no evidence to
demonstrate that “the Defendant can avail herself of any entitlement that
may accrue to Herman Reid.”25 Counsel further submitted that Ms.
Grant’s pleading that, “the Claimant did not disclose to the [R]egistrar of
the High Court the legal status of the deceased at death is simply wrong in
fact and in law”26 carried Ms. Grant’s case no further than the starting
block since, a copy of the Letters of Administration issued to Ms. Greaves
stood in contradiction of that claim.

22 Id. at para. 10.
23 Id. at para. 12.
24 Submissions on Behalf of the Claimant, filed Jul. 30, 2012.Para. 9.
25 Id. at Para. 7.
26 Claimant’s Submissions at para. 25.

Page 10 of 17
[15]
In paragraph 26 of his submissions, Mr. Scotland addressed the purported
Will of Juanita Reid. Mr. Scotland noted that Ms. Grant did not rely on the
Will, which in any event was null and void by virtue of Section 48 of the
Wills and Probate Act which provides that, “the Will is nullified by virtue of
the marriage of the Deceased and the purported Testator.”27

[16]
Mr. Scotland submitted that Mr. Pope did not challenge the Deed of
Assent during his cross examination of Ms. Greaves.28 Nor are there
currently, or have there ever been, any challenges from the heirs of
Herman Reid in relation to the Title of the property. Thus Ms. Greaves
procured the Title for the entire property. These circumstances
considered Mr. Scotland noted that:

The Court is asked to treat the Claimant’s allegations of
absolute entitlement to the subject property as conferred by
the Deed as undisputed and therefore as accepted evidence
definitive of the issues.29

[17]
In regard to Ms. Grant’s treatment of the matter, Mr. Scotland submitted
that her “undesirable attitude towards mitigation as directed by the Court
amounts effectively to a refusal to mitigate.”30 In support of his submission
on this point Mr. Scotland referred the Court to several cases.31 These
cases speak to the conduct of the parties during the course of the litigation
of a matter. Mr. Scotland emphasized these cases in order to highlight the
importance of a litigant’s conduct and the effect of that conduct on costs in

27 Id. at para. 26.
28 Id. at para. 30.
29 Id.
30 Id. at para. 34.
31 ROLF V. DE GUERIN [2011] EWCA Civ 78;
DUNNETT V. RAILTRACK PLC EWCA Civ 302;
HALSEY V. MILTON KEYNES NHS TRUST [2004] EWCA Civ. 576;
JARROM AND SHEPHERD V. SELLARS [2007] EWHC 1366 (CH)

Page 11 of 17
a matter. These cases also demonstrate that the Court does not condone
unreasonable behaviour from litigants.

[18]
In the HALSEY case Lord J. Dyson listed the factors which should be
considered in reviewing litigants’ behaviour and its effect on costs. The
factors include:

(a)
The nature of the dispute;

(b)
The merits of the case;

(c)
Other settlement methods have been attempted;

(d)
The costs of mediation would be disproportionately high;

(e)
Delay; and
(f)
Whether the mediation had a reasonable prospect of
success.32
Mr. Scotland submitted that in spite of the fact that mediation was Court
Ordered, “the Defendant displayed objectionable behaviour and therefore
no effective settlement could be reached outside the Court.”33 Mr.
Scotland reminded the Court that:

The Defendant in this case by their conduct has run the risk
of this Court imposing substantial cost penalties. Additionally
even at the 11th hour during the course of the trial parties
were asked to settle. The Claimant made a proposal without
any counter-offer by the Defendant.34

[19]
Defendant’s Submissions
Mr. Pope submitted that under Section 24(3) of the Administration of
Estate Act Ms. Grant is currently holding Mr. Herman Reid’s share of the
property in Trust.35 Mr. Pope submitted:

32 HALSEY at paras. 16-23.
33 Claimant’s Submissions at para. 37.
34 Id. at para. 39.
35 Legal Submissions, filed on Jul. 31, 2012. Para. 6.

Page 12 of 17

On the death of HERMAN REID, deceased on the 17th
March, 2003, the Claimant’s right to property was in respect
of only one half ½ share of the premises, the remaining one
half ½ share being of the estate of HERMAN REID,
deceased. And as a result, her obtaining a grant of letters of
administration in respect of the premises is questionable,
since she had had no legal relationship to HERMAN REID,
during his lifetime.

On the other hand the Defendant could obtain no right of
property, or at least to the share of property which devolved
to the estate of HERMAN REID. As provided in the
Administration of Estate Act, Chapter 9:01, that share is to
be held in “TRUST” to the benefit of the persons claiming
under the estate of HERMAN REID. And it is submitted that
in the meanwhile the Claimant can enjoy no right of property
in respect of the entire premises.36

Mr. Pope did not submit any legal authorities to buttress his submissions
in this matter.

[20]
ANALYSIS
I will preface my analysis with the sentiment that this matter ought not to
have proceeded to trial, but being a family matter, should have been
settled through mediation. Unfortunately this approach was not
capitalized upon by the parties and the matter proceeded to trial. I note
that the parties attended Community Mediation, came to an agreement but
that the agreement was reneged upon by the Defendant through he
Counsel.

36 Id. at paras. 7-8.

Page 13 of 17
[21]
Defence
The pleadings in this matter were disappointing. Ms. Grant’s Defence
suffered two fatalities; first, her Defence was bare and not supported by
any facts or evidence and second, she did not have the locus standi
required to successfully defend the claim. To make matters worse for Ms.
Grant, she was not permitted to lead any evidence at the trial, leaving her
as a mere observer in her fate, having rejected all opportunities to mediate
the matter. I must agree with Mr. Scotland the on salient issues in this
matter.

[22]
The Defence does not satisfy Part 10.5 CPR
The filed Defence does not meet the requirements of Part 10.5 of the CPR
1998 I agree with Mr. Scotland that Ms. Grant’s Defence was lacking in
important details. He noted that the Defence failed to address some
issues completely and is a bare denial of the allegations set forth in the
claim37. As highlighted by Mr. Scotland, there was not even a challenge of
the title held by Ms. Greaves. I agree entirely and apply the dicta of Jones
J. in ANDRE MARCHONG in which she stated:

The effect of part 10.5 and 10.6 is that a defendant must by
its defence, provide a comprehensive response to the claim
and state its position on each relevant fact or allegation put
forward in the claim in the manner required by the rules...

The rule therefore puts a duty on a defendant to deal with
each fact pleaded against it by either admitting or denying
the facts and will only allow a defendant to avoid that duty
where that defendant has positively stated that he or she
cannot do so because he or she does not know...In my
opinion this accords with the policy of full disclosure and an

37 Claimant’s Submissions at paras. 17 -18.

Page 14 of 17
avoidance of litigation on issues which are unnecessary and
a waste of resources. A defendant can no longer avoid
dealing full frontally with facts by merely requiring them to be
proved and may now only require proof where that defendant
has stated positively and verified by a statement of truth that
the facts cannot be admitted or denied because the
defendant does not know whether they are true or not
(emphasis mine).38

It is clear that the CPR 1998 require Defendants to be vigilant in their
responses. Vague and cryptic defences are not permissible under the
rules so as to ensure that the Court’s resources are fully utilized after
there is full disclosure. Ms. Grant’s Defence does not comply with the full
disclosure requirement.

[23]
Additionally, the Defence purports to allege fraud on Ms. Greaves’s part
yet no facts are pleaded. I say categorically that the requirement that
fraud must be specifically pleaded has not been altered or displaced by
the CPR 1998. In this case Mr. Pope did not even attempt to address this
leg of the Defence in his submissions. In any event, Mr. Scotland did
address the passing allegation of nondisclosure as amounting to fraud by
exhibiting the Grant of Letters of Administration which was issued in
favour of Ms. Greaves. This Grant states Ms. Juanita Reid died,

Intestate leaving Herman Reid her lawful husband who died
on the 17th day of March 2003 without taking upon himself
Letters of Administration of her estate.39

38 ANDRE MARCHONG at para. 10.
39 Statement of Case. Exhibit NJ2. Letters of Administration, filed Feb. 23, 2010.

Page 15 of 17

To my mind, Mr. Scotland has done what was required of him to
effectively displace this claim. Ms. Grant is once again left with empty
hands.

[24]
Locus Standi
Ms. Grant has evidenced no standing which will permit her to defend her
position through Herman Reid. I attempted to elicit from Mr. Pope where
Ms. Grant’s locus standi flowed from in order for her to successfully
defend this matter. Unfortunately however, this information was not
forthcoming. In his submissions to the Court Mr. Pope relied heavily on
the creation of a “TRUST” of Herman Reid’s estate. Without more, Mr.
Pope’s claim that Ms. Grant’s authority to occupy part of the property
stemmed from this “TRUST” fails.

[25]
Ms. Greaves was the only witness presented to the Court in this matter.
During cross examination Ms. Greaves appeared unshaken and confident
in her responses. She gave me no reason to doubt the validity of her
responses.

[26]
COSTS
Parties are constrained by the CPR 1998 to assist the Court in furthering
the Overriding Objective. This entails making use of ADR measures as
available to settle their matters. In this instance the parties availed
themselves of Mediation Services but for the reason that the Defendant
reneged on the Agreement, the matter ended up in trial. This behaviour
cannot be condoned and in this case the opprobrium of the court shall be
reflected in an Order for costs.

[27]
CONCLUSION:

The facts of the matter remain that although Ms. Grant’s mother’s name is
mentioned in Juanita Reid’s Will, she predeceased Mrs. Reid so that the

Page 16 of 17
gift lapsed. In addition, that Will predated Mrs. Reid’s marriage to Herman
Reid so that is ineffective. There is no blood or familial relationship
existing between Mr. Herman Reid and Ms. Grant so that for our
purposes, she is a stranger to him and no “TRUST” therefore exists.
When all is therefore taken into account, Ms. Grant is bereft of any leg to
defend these proceedings.

[28]
In view of the matter as it progressed from CMC to trial, I am of the view
that the Defendant has no discernible defence to this case and is
trespassing upon the Claimant’s property. The Defendant also has no
standing which would permit her to claim possession of a portion of the
property through Herman Reid. Consequently, the Defendant must vacate
the property.

IT IS HEREBY ORDERED AS FOLLOWS:

1.
That the Defendants’ Defence to the Claim filed on April 12, 2010
be and is hereby struck out on the ground of disclosing no
defence.

2.
That the Statement of Case filed on February 23, 2010 be and is
hereby granted.

3.
That the Defendant has 60 days from the date of this order to
remove herself and her belongings from the property.

4.
That the Defendant do pay the Claimant’s costs to be assessed if
not agreed.

5.
That the Claimant do file her Statement of Costs on or before
October 12, 2012.

6.
That the Defendant do file and serve her response on or before
October 26, 2012.

Page 17 of 17
7.
That Assessment do take place on November 7, 2012 at 10am in
POS 17.

Dated this 28th day of September 2012.
